Ainsworth's Historical Romances follow in twenty volumes, published at $300 and offered here at $100.00. The catalogue itself is the whole work: a bookseller's priced inventory of sets, illustrated books and standard authors for collectors ordering by mail.
47126-why-we-punctuate-or-reason-versus-:
William Livingston Klein's Why We Punctuate, or Reason versus Rule in the Use of Marks, reached a second edition, entirely rewritten, from the Lancet Publishing Company at Minneapolis in 1916. Klein dedicates the book to his wife, who discussed the intricate and often dull problems of punctuation with him for years.

The chapters treat the functions of marks, grouping as the fundamental purpose of punctuation, parenthesis and appositives, and the grouping done by the semicolon and the colon. Later chapters separate comma, semicolon, colon, and period, then comma, dash, and parentheses, before quotation-marks, brackets, compound words, and close and open punctuation. An announcement promises a briefer handbook, keeping the reasons for the use of marks but dropping most of the discussion.
48461-husks:
Marion Harland wrote this novel, Husks, issued at New York as a ten-cent number in a cheap fiction library. Chapter one opens on a decided, uncompromising rainy day. No showers teased by shifting winds, but a uniform spread of iron-gray cloud and straight lines of heavy rain on the earth.

Naked trees shiver for their early leaf-buds, gutters run as brimming streams, and sidewalks glaze with thin sheets of water. The tale then pauses before a block of houses that a knowing eye would read at once: highly respectable, even in the rain. On a clear day its blinds show lace and silk, its children trip after hoops, and fine carriages discharge their loads at the brown-stone fronts. Other streets offer larger houses for the same price, the narrator notes, but the block's own people vote them wanting in style.
49127-brahms-and-some-of-his-works:
Brahms and Some of His Works is a concert guide by Pitts Sanborn, printed at New York in 1940. Sanborn wrote it for the radio members of the Philharmonic-Symphony Society of New York, and dedicated it to them. A portrait of Johannes Brahms serves as frontispiece. The life opens in the then free city of Hamburg.

Brahms was born there on May 7, 1833, in humble circumstances, in a poor part of the city. His father was a well-trained musician and an accomplished double-bass player. His mother, seventeen years the father's senior, was a woman of fine spirit and unusual intelligence. At six the boy began the rudiments of music from his father, who meant to make an orchestral player of him. Sanborn tells the life as a road into the works.
49271-common-minerals-and-rocks:
Common Minerals and Rocks, by William Crosby, is a teaching guide issued by the Boston Society of Natural History. It forms number twelve in a series of guides for science teaching. The introduction sets minerals and rocks as the field matter of geology. Crosby splits geology into three great divisions that match the divisions of biology.

The first division studies the forces now at work on and in the earth. Oceans, rivers, rain, frost, volcanoes, and earthquakes fall under that head. The second studies the rocks and structures those forces have produced over past ages. The third, historical geology, reads the earth's story in the order of its layers. Crosby limits this short course to the first two divisions alone. The aim is a clear sketch of rock forming forces and rock kinds.
49368-the-political-institutions-of-the-:
The Political Institutions of the Ancient Greeks is a work of comparative politics by Basil Hammond, fellow and lecturer of Trinity College, Cambridge. Clay and Sons published it for the Cambridge University Press in 1895. Hammond's preface explains that these chapters are not a whole by themselves. They are an enlarged version of one part of a lecture course on European political institutions, treated historically and comparatively.

He hopes to enlarge the other parts of the course in the same way and append them, making this only a first instalment of a book on comparative politics. The pages give a description and examination of Greek governments. A passage preserved in the copy engages Herbert Spencer's Political Institutions. Hammond grants that Spencer placed the study of non-European governments on a scientific footing.
49431-the-burial-customs-of-the-ancient-:
Frank Pierrepont Graves wrote The Burial Customs of the Ancient Greeks as a dissertation at Columbia College, issued at Brooklyn in May 1891. Graves makes no claim to profound scholarship. His preface owns that errors may be visible to any careful student of Greek archaeology.

The material, he explains, lay scattered through ancient and modern authors, excavation reports, and museum treasures. He gathered it into one connected account, hoping to breed interest in the subject. His authorities list ranges from Becker's Charicles to the great corpus of Greek inscriptions. The thesis treats how the Greeks buried and mourned their dead: the rites, the tombs, and the beliefs behind them, as a young scholar of 1891 could assemble them.
49919-catalogue-of-s-w-partridge-co-s-po:
Partridge's catalogue of popular illustrated books is the trade list of S W Partridge and Company, classified according to prices. New books and new editions are marked with an asterisk. The list is a window on the Victorian market for improving and adventurous reading.

At 5s each stand large crown octavos in cloth extra. Eliza F Pollard's A Hero King, a romance of Alfred the Great, stands there, and her Gentleman of England from the days of Sir Philip Sidney. The Dacoit's Treasure, a prize story of Burmese life, and Sarah Doudney's Pilgrims of the Night share the shelf. G Manville Fenn fills a block alone: Jungle and Stream, Cormorant Crag, In Honour's Cause, Steve Young. At 3s 6d come more Fenn, a Henty adventure medley, and Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress with fifty-five engravings. Daily meditations and hymn writers serve the serious buyer.
50258-mendelssohn-and-certain-masterwork:
Herbert Peyser wrote Mendelssohn and Certain Masterworks for the radio members of the Philharmonic-Symphony Society of New York, copyrighted in 1947. A sketch of Mendelssohn by Carl Mueller, dated 1842, stands at the front. The tale opens far behind the composer, in 1729, the year of Bach's St Matthew Passion. In Dessau on the Elbe, a poor Jew named Mendel becomes father of a boy called Moses.

Mendel kept a small Hebrew day-school and copied out the Pentateuch for a living. He rose before dawn in winter to carry his son, wrapped in a shawl, to Rabbi David Frankel's school. Moses proved a gifted pupil with a restless thirst to know. The Guide of the Perplexed shaped him deeply, though hard study warped his spine for life.
50374-the-life-and-labors-of-elias-hicks:
The Life and Labors of Elias Hicks is a life of the famed priest of the Friends whose name split that sect, by Wilbur. A co hand is named on its title page. It came out at Philadelphia in the first years of the last age, from a board of that sect.

Its rights were held that year by its chief hand. Its parts take his blood and boy days first, then his young man days. His first stand in the priest craft, his first works, and his late works fill the next run. His faith trips of a set year, his views on the priest craft, and his home and kin come next. His notes to his wife, the slave ask, and his points of faith lead to the split.
50665-auguste-rodin-the-man-his-ideas-hi:
Camille Mauclair wrote this study of Auguste Rodin, Englished by Clementina Black. Dutton printed the book in New York in 1905 with forty plates. Mauclair gives the book to painter Eugene Carriere and critic Roger Marx. Both men had backed Rodin from his earliest hard years.

Part one traces youth, first work, and time in Brussels at Carrier shop. The Age of Brass at the Salon of 1877 sparked a sharp row. Saint John the Baptist then began Rodin lasting fame in France. Part two treats the studio, Eve, busts, and the Gate of Hell.
50793-cousin-lucy-s-conversations-by-the:
Cousin Lucy's Conversations belongs to the Lucy Books, a series for girls by the author of the Rollo Books. The text here is a new edition, revised by the author and printed in New York in 1854. Lucy, Rollo's cousin, learns through talks and small daily events rather than through formal lessons.

Fourteen conversations make up the book. Their subjects range from a treasury and a glen to getting lost, sketching, and a talk held at midnight. A short notice at the front explains the plan behind the series. The Rollo Books had shown the daily life of a boy, and these volumes extend the same approach to his cousin. The stories aim to amuse young readers while quietly teaching care, honesty, and good sense.
50821-the-causes-of-the-successes-of-the:
The Causes of the Successes of the Ottoman Turks is the Stanhope Prize Essay for 1859. James Surtees Phillpotts, a scholar of New College, wrote it, and it was printed at Oxford the same year. Phillpotts asks how a small clan of Turks grew into the power that took Constantinople and pressed deep into Europe. His answer begins in the wreck of the Seljuk order in Asia Minor.

The essay follows Ertogruhl's Oghouz clan, settled in Phrygia by the chief of Iconium. It then follows his son Othman, who made himself an independent chieftain on the Greek border. Orchan's gains in Bithynia came next, opened by the Emperor Michael's ill-judged saving on the mountain militia. Phillpotts weighs race, faith, and arms together, in the manner of a young Oxford historian explaining an empire's rise.
51145-asmodeus-or-the-devil-on-two-stick:
Asmodeus, or The Devil on Two Sticks, by Le Sage, appears in a London edition of 1879. Routledge issued the book in London and New York. Joseph Thomas made this translation. Tony Johannot drew the pictures. A life of the author by Jules Janin stands at the front. The picture shows Asmodeus and Zambullo flying over Madrid. Thomas says he first meant only to revise the old English version. A few pages changed his mind. The old rendering lacked style, he charges, though the French sings.

Le Sage ranks, for Thomas, among the great masters of verbal melody. Gil Blas won British love while this tale stayed undervalued. Thomas blames the dress, not the work. He strove to carry the ideas over with their wit intact. The preface is a small essay on what translation owes a classic.
5133-quotations-from-john-l-motley-works:
This small volume gathers quotations from John Lothrop Motley's History of the Netherlands, selected by the Project Gutenberg editor David Widger. Motley's history, a classic of nineteenth-century American scholarship, tells the Dutch struggle against Spain for independence and religious freedom.

The quotations are arranged for readers who want Motley's most striking passages without reading the whole history at once, and the editor invites suggestions for favourite passages to add. The book works as a tasting menu for Motley's prose and as a quick reference for students of the Dutch revolt.
51332-to-the-fore-with-the-tanks:
To the Fore with the Tanks, a boys' adventure novel by Percy Westerman, takes its hero to the front in the Great War. It was first published in 1917 by Partridge of London and was often reprinted. The book belongs to a series of war adventure tales. Westerman also wrote The Airship Golden Hind and The Secret Battleplane.

The chapters run in brisk order: To the Front, The Communication Trench, The Night Attack, and Grub. Then come an expedition to no man's land, a prisoner of war, and the first advance. The tale is told for boys who followed the war in the papers and wanted it brought close. Tanks were a new and secret weapon when the book came out, and the story trades on that wonder. Westerman was one of the most prolific writers of boys' war and sea tales of his time.
51962-bill-nye-s-sparks:
Edgar Wilson Nye, known as Bill Nye, fills a humor volume issued at New York and Chicago in 1896. A life sketch opens the book, tracing Nye from a poor boyhood in Maine to school teaching in Wisconsin. At twenty-five he taught a district school for thirty dollars a month.

The sketch tells how Nye became a justice of the peace at Laramie, unpaid save by fees and once too poor to mail letters for three weeks. Letters to a Cheyenne paper won him a post on the Laramie Sentinel at twelve dollars a week. There his free hand with facts and his warm manner won every heart, the sketch claims. Readers get the humor pieces of a western newspaperman whose dry manner made him a national name.
52860-our-story-book-jingles-stories-and:
Our Story Book, Jingles, Stories and Rhymes for Little Folks, was issued at New York in 1916 by Cupples and Leon Company with many pictures. A verse on little drops of water heads the book. Wideawake Willy leads the contents. The Little Old Woman and Funny Toys follow in the list.

Seven Froggies of Lee and Tinklebell Tales sit in the early part. The Twins, Five Little Frogs, and Dickie and Daisy fill the middle. The Fox That Lost His Tail teaches not to follow each fashion. The Cats and the Cheese teaches to agree rather than go to law. Tommy's First Day at School and a Day at the Farm close the run of short pieces. Short morals in plain tales suit the youngest readers at home.
5348-ragged-dick-or-street-life-in-new-y:
Horatio Alger's Ragged Dick, or Street Life in New York, introduces Dick, a bootblack of the streets. Its chapters follow Johnny Nolan, Dick's new suit, Chatham Street and Broadway, a pocket-book, and Dick's early history. Later chapters bring a scene in a Third Avenue car, Dick as a detective, a room on Mott Street, and Micky Maguire.

Alger's most famous hero rises by honesty, pluck, and a tutor's help, in the rags-to-respectability pattern that made Alger a byword. The book offers young readers a lively portrait of old New York street life. It remains the classic statement of the Alger myth of self-help.
53788-elizabeth-her-folks:
Barbara Kay wrote a girls' tale, Elizabeth, Her Folks, issued at Garden City in 1920 with drawings by the Donaldsons. It belongs to a small series that began with Elizabeth and her books. The first chapter, John's Girl, opens with Elizabeth sobbing across the foot of Grandmother Swift's great guest-chamber bed.

Downstairs, her grandparents rock before the windows and talk the newcomer over. Grandmother thinks her pale and peaked, but pleased, and fond of the chocolate cake especially. Grandfather jokes that he never saw a brown berry, though she says they will soon have the girl brown as one. Chapters ahead bring a bean supper, a locked closet, and letters at the post office.
53903-catalogue-of-practical-scientific-:
Henry Carey Baird and Company of Philadelphia issued this catalogue of practical and scientific books for sale by mail. The firm stood at 810 Walnut Street and traced its start to Mathew Carey in 1785. Any book listed could be sent free of postage at the printed price. A larger descriptive catalogue of 96 pages was sent free on request.

Entries run in order by author, with size and price for each. Titles cover varnishes, coach painting, steam boilers, and weaving. Others deal with cotton spinning, paper hanging, and long span bridges. Prices range from cents to ten dollars for large plate works. The list is a window on the trade in how-to science books of its day.
54731-the-sieges-of-vienna-by-the-turks:
The Sieges of Vienna by the Turks retells the two great Ottoman sieges of the Austrian capital. The Earl of Ellesmere translated the account from the German of Karl August Schimmer and other sources, and John Murray of London issued this new edition in 1879. A plan of Vienna with the Turkish approaches forms the frontispiece.

Ellesmere names his authorities in the preface. Schimmer, a resident of Vienna with access to its archives, supplied the groundwork. Von Hammer's Turkish history, Coyer's Life of Sobieski, Salvandy's History of Poland, and Sobieski's own letters served for addition and checking. Verses at the front tell how Sobieski turned the Muslim to flight from Vienna's walls. The book is a Victorian Englishman's tribute to the Polish king who saved the city in 1683.
54752-catalogue-of-practical-and-scienti:
Catalogue of Practical and Scientific Books is a price list from Henry Carey Baird, a publisher of trade books at Philadelphia. Baird styles himself an industrial publisher, with his shop on Walnut Street. Any book in the list could be sent by mail, free of postage, at the printed price.

The list opens with a draughtsman's book of industrial design, a full course in drawing for engineers. That large work, with one hundred plates and cuts, sold for ten dollars. A paper-hanger's companion, with rules for pastes, damp walls, and the dressing of rooms, went for a dollar and a quarter. A cotton spinner's guide gives sizes and speeds of machines, with twist sums and rules for changes. The list runs on in that vein for many trades.
56113-irrigation-works:
E S Bellasis, lately superintending engineer in the irrigation branch of the Public Works Department of India, wrote Irrigation Works, issued at London and New York by Spon in 1913. The book sets out the rules on which the design and working of such works should rest, with special detail on Indian canals. Thirty-seven pictures aid the text, and a bridge on an Indian canal stands at the front.

The chapters run from first remarks and the chief rules of canal design through losses of water, the duty of water, and the sketch of a project. Then come headworks, contour maps, alignments, branches, banks, outlets, masonry works, and pitching. Bellasis had also written on river and canal work, Punjab rivers, and hydraulics with tables. The book is a working manual by a man who had run great canals.
57325-artful-anticks:
Artful Anticks, by Oliver Herford, is a book of comic verse and pictures. The Century firm of New York issued the gathered work in nineteen o one. Rights run from eighteen eighty eight through the next six years. Herford pieces first ran in the Century over that long span.

Contents promise the Audacious Kitten, the Artful Ant, and the Gifted Ant. Sir Rat is billed as a comedy among the short verse tales. The Geometrical Giraffe, the Early Owl, and the Forgetful Forget Me Not follow. An Elf and the Dormouse, a Spider Tale, and a Parrot and Cuckoo close in. Light fables of beasts and elves fill the book for young readers.
5831-the-riches-of-bunyan-selected-from-:
Jeremiah Chaplin selects devotional passages from John Bunyan in The Riches of Bunyan, prepared for the American Tract Society and published in New York in 1850. William Williams supplies an introductory notice, and contents open with God in glory, majesty, justice, and holiness, before moving through further themes of faith. The selections draw on Bunyan's wider works beyond his famous allegory.

Readers get Bunyan as a preacher and comforter, in short passages suited to daily reading and meditation. The book favors plain, earnest prose over argument, letting Scripture and experience speak together. It suits readers of Puritan devotion, Bunyan lovers, and anyone seeking a compact anthology of seventeenth-century spiritual writing.
58491-the-golden-boys-with-the-lumber-ja:
The Golden Boys With the Lumber Jacks, by Wyman, is a tale for boys of twelve to sixteen. Burt issued the book in New York with a copyright of 1923. Wyman, dean of the Pennsylvania Military College, wrote a whole series on the same boys.

The first chapter strands the party in snow: their sedan grinds to a stop despite chains on the rear wheels. Wind roars and drives blinding snow against the windows as the driver is told they are stuck. The chapters bring a lost deed and a ghost at the lumber camp. The ghost has its picture taken, and Tom lays it in due course. Big Ben makes a call and falls down again, and a man named Jacques Lamont hides a secret. Jack takes a forced walk before the tale ends.
58866-the-murder-on-the-links:
The Murder on the Links, by Agatha Christie, is dedicated to her husband, a fellow enthusiast for detective stories, to whom she owed much helpful advice and criticism. Contents open with a fellow traveller, then an appeal for help, and a arrival at the Villa Genevieve.

A letter signed Bella, Mrs Renauld story, and the scene of the crime follow. A mysterious Madame Daubreuil, an unexpected meeting, and a rival detective who finds some clues fill the middle. Poirot elucidates certain points, one title says, and later: I use my grey cells. A second body and a photograph are listed. The girl with the anxious eyes closes the list. Chapter one opens in early June, on a train from Paris to London, with a mock anecdote about a duchess. Readers get an early Poirot novel, all method and misdirection.
59058-aristotle-s-history-of-animals-in-:
Richard Cresswell of Saint John's College, Oxford, translated Aristotle's History of Animals in Ten Books, published in London in 1887. His preface says the translation was made from the text of Schneider, whose notes he consulted throughout. In difficult places he compared the English of Taylor, the French of Camus, and the German of Strack.

Cresswell hopes errors that escaped him are neither numerous nor important. The work itself he calls the most ambitious of Aristotle's animal studies, a great survey of kinds, parts, habits, and generation. Readers get the founding text of zoology in a Victorian scholarly translation, with the translator's method stated plainly.
59900-the-mud-larks:
Crosbie Garstin, a lieutenant in the First King Edward's Horse, wrote sketches of cavalry life at the front, printed in New York in 1919. He gives the book to the memory of his brother, Captain Denis Norman Garstin, killed in action near Archangel in Russia on August 17, 1918. A verse waves beyond the stars that all is well.

Chapters tell of the padre, the riding master, horse sense, and the regimental mascot. A mule meets a tank in one sketch. Leave, war paint, the pinch of war, and funny cuts fill others. One schoolboy effort on the noble ferret gets stuck at its nobility. Humor and grief share these pages of horse soldiers at war.
60624-two-whole-glorious-weeks:
Two Whole Glorious Weeks, by Will Worthington, was printed from Worlds of If Science Fiction of October 1958. A head note calls it a new author's strange view of the summer camp of the future. Hard labor, insults, and hog kidneys wait there, it warns. Rain of a fine, keen sort soaks the pair on the way in.

Bertha and the teller reach Morton's place past two blowouts on a rough road. Folk in gray suits dig stumps waist deep in swamp water by the camp. A high fence with barbed wire rings thirty acres of swamp, a rock quarry, a jute mill, and a steam laundry. A board at the gate bans talk and smoke. The camp calls itself Morton's Misery Farm, with the harshest food laws in the Catskills. Readers get a sly tale of rest by torment.
60929-our-national-parks:
John Muir wrote Our National Parks from sketches first printed in the Atlantic Monthly. His preface is dated at Martinez in September 1901. Muir says he did his best to show the beauty and use of the wild parks and woods. He hoped folk would come, take them to heart, and so keep them safe for good. Photographs by Herbert Gleason fill the book, from high peaks to falls and big trees. Tables in the back were built by Allen Chamberlain from state sources.

Inside, Muir walks through Yellowstone, Yosemite, and the Sierra Nevada in fond detail. He writes of bears, deer, trout streams, snow in June, and giant sequoia groves. A map shows the parks and reserves of the day. The book is both a guide and a plea, from a man who knew these wild lands on foot.
61317-reflections-on-the-painting-and-sc:
Reflections on the Painting and Sculpture of the Greeks is Fuseli's translation of Winckelmann's famous essay. Winckelmann, librarian of the Vatican, had published the German original ten years earlier. The volume adds instructions for the connoisseur and an essay on grace in works of art.

The opening argument made modern taste. To the Greek climate, Winckelmann says, we owe the production of taste itself; foreign inventions were mere seeds that changed their nature in that chosen soil. There is but one way for moderns to become great, and perhaps unequalled: by imitating the ancients. Raphael sent young artists to Greece to copy the remains. An ancient Roman statue beside a Greek one, he warns, will look like Virgil beside Homer. Fuseli's translation carried the gospel of Greek art into English at the start of the classical revival.
61345-companionable-books:
Henry Van Dyke commends great reading in Companionable Books, published at New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in October 1922 and dedicated to Maxwell Struthers Burt. A Keats portrait by Joseph Severn fronts the volume. Twelve chapters begin with the Book of Books and poetry in the Psalms, then turn to the good enchantment of Dickens.

Thackeray and real men, George Eliot and real women, Keats the poet of immortal youth and Wordsworth's recovery of joy follow. Browning, Walton by quiet streams, Samuel Johnson, Emerson and Stevenson close the company, and Margaret Armstrong's cover assigns each author a symbolic flower.
61432-forest-pictures-in-the-adirondacks:
John Hows made pictures of the Adirondack forests, with original poems by Alfred Street, in a book printed in New York in 1865. Bobbett and Hooper engraved the plates. Each picture pairs with a poem on the same scene. At Rest opens the set, as a soft southwest wind bids the camper rest on nature's breast.

Rapids, shallows, waterfalls, and cataracts follow. The Lower and Upper Saranac, the Ausable, and Buttermilk Falls each get a plate and verses. A mountain raven, a bell owl, and a loon give wild life its turn. Camp fire light, hemlock beds, and panther cries in the dark make a rich album of the northern woods for parlor readers.
61689-the-home-life-of-the-ancient-greek:
The Home Life of the Ancient Greeks is a study by Blumner, translated by Alice Zimmern. Cassell issued the new and revised edition in 1895. Zimmern was a late scholar of Girton College, Cambridge. Her preface explains the translation's method. It is not word for word, she says. It aims to give the author's sense in clear English dress. A Greek lady at her toilet serves as frontispiece.

The contents begin with costume, then birth and infancy. Education and marriage follow in their turn. House, food, and daily custom fill the later parts. Illustrations are taken from the German original. A list of authorities closes the book. Blumner drew on vases, plays, and household goods. Such works made the ancient world a place of homes. English readers gained a full picture of Greek daily life.
61770-dorymates-a-tale-of-the-fishing-ba:
Dorymates is a tale of the fishing banks by Kirk Munroe. He wrote past boys books of the south seas and the wilds. It came out at New York and London in the early nineteen hundreds. Its form holds pictures through the text. A note tells how the print copy was set, with notes moved to sit by the text.

A front plate shows a small lad who grins up into a worn face. That face is hard from wind and sea. The tale form is plain from its title and plate. Two mates work a dory boat on the great banks. Small boats leave the mother ship there to haul fish in fog and storm. Peril, pluck, and the bond of the boat drive a boys sea tale.
61777-journal-of-the-life-and-religious-:
The Journal of the Life and Religious Labours of Elias Hicks, written by himself, was published by Isaac T Hopper in New York in 1832. A preface explains that Hicks left several manuscripts among his papers, and that his connexions have collected these memoirs for the public. The editors call the record of his long and useful life animating and instructive.

The contents begin with his birth in 1748, early visitations of divine grace, apprenticeship, trials, and marriage in 1771. There follows his appearance in the ministry and a long roll of journeys. He travels to Philadelphia in 1779, to Nine Partners in 1783, into New England and Vermont in 1793, and to Canada in 1803.
63128-rudimentary-treatise-on-the-constr:
Charles Tomlinson edited this treatise on how locks are built and judged. John Weale printed the book in London in 1853. A French quote from Reaumur heads the work with praise of locks. It calls locks true machines, common yet little understood by users.

Most folk judge a lock by its outside face alone, it notes. Few know what makes a lock good or how safe it is. Plates show the inner works of locks in fine detail. The book serves smiths, builders, and all who guard homes and goods. Readers learn how tumblers, bolts, and keys fit and work.
63237-early-printed-books:
Early Printed Books, by Gordon Duff, was published in London in 1893. Kegan Paul and partners issued the volume. Duff gives the book to the memory of Henry Bradshaw. A page from Schoeffer's Canon of the Mass, printed about 1458, fronts the work. Thirteen chapters make the survey. Steps towards the invention come first, then the invention of printing itself. The spread of the art runs country by country: Germany, Italy, France, and the Low Countries. Spain, Portugal, Denmark, and Sweden share a chapter.

Westminster takes the next, with Caxton and Wynkyn de Worde. Oxford and St Albans follow, then the London printers. Bookbinding and the collecting of early books close the text. An index of printers and places ends the volume. Duff writes the standard short history of the fifteenth century press.
63907-weale-s-series-of-scientific-and-t:
Weale Series of Scientific and Technical Works is a classified publisher list, issued in London in 1900. Crosby Lockwood and Son published the list from Stationers Hall Court that year. A notice from the Engineer, quoted at its head, praises the series in strong terms. No books, it says, have ever proved more popular or more useful to young engineers.

The classified heads divide the little treatises by their crafts for the buyer. Civil engineering and surveying open the list at page two. Mining and metallurgy, mechanical engineering, and navigation and shipbuilding follow in the contents. Architecture and building, industrial and useful arts, and agriculture and gardening come next in order. Weale rudimentary treatises were the self education of the Victorian engineer in shilling volumes. This list is their catalogue and their monument: hundreds of small books by which clerks and fitters taught themselves a profession.
64207-of-medicine-in-eight-books:
Celsus's Of Medicine in Eight Books, in Greive's translation with critical and explanatory notes, appears here in a new edition printed at Edinburgh in 1814 for Dickinson and Company. Greive's dedication, dated from London in January 1756, addresses Sharp, surgeon to Guy's Hospital, who revised the surgical part.

His preface takes up the old question whether ancient physicians can guide modern practice. The body's mechanism, he argues, is always and everywhere the same, so a faithful history of diseases must be among the surest guides to proper remedies. Diagnosis and prognosis, the greatest matters in physic, rest on long and accurate observation, and in that the ancients were assiduous, clear and exact.
64216-tad-coon-s-tricks:
John Breck wrote these animal tales, Tad Coon's Tricks, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1923 with pictures by William Andrews. The book sits in the Told at Twilight Stories, most of them about Nibble the Bunny. Sister volumes give Nibble more friends and Silvertip the Fox his sins. A front picture shows Tad sending a big rock down on Grandpop Snapping Turtle.

Contents open with Songs of the Hunt, then Tad's tricks and his troubles. Grandpop's bite that never let go and tricks coming home to roost follow. Tad makes a compact with Watch and Tommy Peele, and Nibble turns detective after a crime in the hen house. Stripes Skunk learns how to behave, and Doctor Muskrat tells why skunks are so.
64306-artificial-fire-works:
Robert Jones, an artillery officer, wrote this guide to making fireworks. The second form came out in London in 1766 with plates. Jones covers the craft from the smallest to the highest branch. About a hundred figures are cut on copper for the book.

Lists name rockets, wheels, fountains, gerbes, and gold rain effects. Jones gives mixes, tools, moulds, and steps to make each piece. He also tells how to refine saltpetre for the work. Water fireworks, sea fights, and swans show the full range of the art in that age.
64514-goya-an-account-of-his-life-and-wo:
Albert F Calvert wrote Goya, an account of his life and works put out in London and New York in 1908. The book sits in a set on Spain, with books on Toledo, Seville, and El Greco. It holds 612 copies of his work in all. Paint, etched plates, and stone prints fill that count.

Calvert gave the book to the Marquis of Comillas. He praises the marquis as a friend of art and of Spain. The plates start with The Family of Charles the Fourth, held at the Prado in Madrid. Court faces of the princes of that house follow in a row. Church paint, the bull ring, and the dark late works fill the list. The book serves as a life, a guide to the rooms that hold his work, and a shelf of plates.
64627-athletics-and-games-of-the-ancient:
Athletics and Games of the Ancient Greeks, by Edward Plummer, was reprinted from the American Physical Education Review of 1898 and printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Plummer was an ear surgeon at a Boston hospital and an instructor at the Boston Polyclinic. Part one treats athletic games among the Homeric heroes.

Few kinds of labour develop the body in a symmetrical manner, he opens. Even in an elementary division of labour this holds. The carpenter and blacksmith usually have strong, large shoulders and arms, but small and weak legs. If primitive labour does this, modern labourers show it more, he argues. Greek athletics enter as the contrast. Readers get a short 1898 lecture linking Homer games to modern physical training.
64985-men-women-and-books:
Augustine Birrell's Men, Women, and Books, essays about men, women, and books, was published in London by Elliot Stock in 1910. A publisher's list of Birrell's other works, Obiter Dicta and In the Name of the Bodleian among them, fronts the title page.

The contents open with literary lives: Dean Swift, Lord Bolingbroke, Sterne, Doctor Johnson, Richard Cumberland, Hannah More, and Marie Bashkirtseff. Essays on Sir John Vanbrugh, John Gay, and Roger North's autobiography follow, then pieces on books old and new, book-binding, poets laureate, and parliamentary candidates. The first essay begins by refusing to complain that books about Dean Swift are endless, since the subject must always remain one of strange fascination.
65248-the-murderous-tyranny-of-the-turks:
Arnold Toynbee wrote this pamphlet in 1917, with a preface by Viscount Bryce, sold in New York for five cents. Its title quotes the Allied governments' joint note to President Wilson, pledging the liberation of peoples under Turkish rule and the expulsion of the Ottoman Empire from Europe.

Quotations from Gladstone and Treitschke frame the case before Bryce's preface begins. Bryce says no student of five centuries of Near Eastern history will be surprised at the Allied purpose. Readers get wartime advocacy at its most direct: a young historian marshaling history to argue that Ottoman rule in Europe must end.
67329-charles-robert-maturin-his-life-an:
Charles Robert Maturin is a scholarly life and study by Niilo Idman. It was presented as a thesis at Helsingfors in 1923. Idman gathered most of his material in 1914. War then cut him off from England for years. He could not check or add to his notes. The preface owns these gaps with frankness. Maturin's sway on French romantic writing is left aside.

His mark on later English letters is only sketched. Still, Maturin's own works fill the study. Even the minor ones are reviewed at length. They had vanished from print long before, Idman notes. Maturin wrote Melmoth the Wanderer, a Gothic peak. His plays and novels mirror his wild age. Idman's book is a patient work of rescue.
67553-etiquette-for-little-folks:
A small manners book for children lays down rules for good acts at home. The book came out in Boston, its rights filed in 1856. It sits in the Susie Sunbeam set for the young. A plate shows a woman with two children at its front. Home rules lead its list of themes in plain words.

Come in with no hat on, and bow to guests in the house. Bow to your parents when you pass them, at home or out. If they talk with guests, hold your ask till they are free. If you must speak, then speak in a low hiss of words. Call them Sir or Madam in each word you say. Quick heed to their word is the core rule here.
67570-the-play-day-book-new-stories-for-:
Fanny Fern wrote The Play-Day Book, new stories for little folks, printed at New York in 1857. Fred Coffin drew the pictures. Fern's preface says children wrote asking for another book after Little Ferns, and here it is.

She made the book for play days, out of school hours, hoping lessons might slip in with the fun. More than forty short pieces follow: A Rainy Day, The Circus, Katy's First Grief, and History of a Family of Cats. Tales of a cripple, a tom-boy, a poor-rich child, and a lucky Irish boy fill the list. A temperance story and a Thanksgiving piece close the set.
67601-cousin-lucy-at-study-by-the-author:
The author of the Rollo Books wrote a companion series for girls, the Lucy Books, of which this volume is a revised edition of 1854. Earlier volumes were Cousin Lucy's Conversations and Cousin Lucy's Stories. The preface hopes small readers will be both interested and profited by the perusal.

Lucy is about five when her mother comes home from the city with a thin, flat parcel for her, a new slate. Her brother Royal teases to open it for her, but Lucy wants to open it herself. Chapters follow on accounts, a wagon ride, a magazine, and the theory of interruption. Study, for Lucy, is a moral exercise as much as a school one.
67689-cousin-lucy-at-play-by-the-author-:
Clark, Austin and Smith issued a new edition in New York in 1857 of a tale for girls by the author of the Rollo Books. The Lucy Books were meant as a match for the Rollo Books for boys. Two earlier Lucy books held talks and tales, and this one joins a twin book on study.

Lucy and her brother Royal share a painted wood box, called the marble box, full of books and playthings. Their mother keeps the key on a blue ribbon, and the box may open only when the children get well after illness. Chapters bring a ride to town, a gypsy party, a lone sleigh ride, and a fright.
68103-twenty-years-at-sea-leaves-from-my:
Frederic Stanhope Hill recalls a sailor's life in Twenty Years at Sea, or leaves from my old log books, printed at Boston and New York in 1893. Houghton Mifflin made the book. Hill gives it to his wife, to whose suggestion the publication of these episodes in a life is due, he says.

Two parts divide the years. Part one, in the merchant service, runs from how I went to sea and my first voyage. The mutiny, not born to be drowned, and a shanghaeing episode follow. To California before the gold discovery, recapturing a runaway, and chased by pirates close the half. Part two, in the naval service, opens with the outbreak of the Civil War. A night attack by a Confederate ram, the passage of the forts and capture of New Orleans, and chasing a blockade runner fill it. The end of the struggle closes the book.
68367-the-devil-s-picture-books:
Mrs John King Van Rensselaer wrote The Devil's Picture-Books, a history of playing-cards dated eighteen ninety. Dodd, Mead and Company issued the book at New York, with pictures. The preface explains the odd title.

Puritans, she says, called cards the Devil's Books to scare timid folk from using them. Whether the Devil made cards, no one can know. Learned men had written on cards before her, and she names La Croix, Chatto, Taylor, and Singer. Their books were out of print and hard to get. She gathers their chief facts into a small compass. Staff at a Washington museum helped her hunt rare packs.
68873-a-century-of-children-s-books:
A Century of Children's Books, by Florence Barry, is a history of the field, published by Methuen of London in 1922. Chapters run from chap-books and ballads to fairy tales and Eastern stories. Appendices add notes and extracts, and a chronological list.

Middle chapters treat the Lilliputian Library, Rousseau and the moral tale, and Rousseau's English school. Then come devices of the moralist, great writers of little books, and Edgeworth's tales. The first chapter opens with Steele's Tatler account of his two god-children. The boy, a great historian in Aesop's fables, said he did not believe them true. He had detected the man inside the lion's skin, pointing the moral. His sister Betty dealt in fairies and sprites, and terrified the maids.
68926-stories-and-ballads-for-young-folk:
Ellen Tracy Alden wrote a miscellany of stories and ballads for young folks, copyrighted in 1879 and issued at New York in 1880. Its contents run from tales like Neighbor Edith, Castle Marvel, and Patches and Perseverance to short rhymes of a page or two, ending with Bobbie and the Bee. A centennial tea-pot and a child on the battle-field stand among them.

The first story opens on a snowy afternoon: a lieutenant, blinded and one-handed, lies sunk in gloomy reverie on a lounge, calling himself a shattered, helpless wreck. His little neighbour climbs silently behind him and showers kisses over his sightless eyes, laughing that she surprised him. Home sentiment and fairy tale share the volume equally.
69043-chair-backs:
Chair Backs is a crochet pattern booklet, Star Book number forty six, sold for ten cents. The American Thread Company of New York published it to sell its crochet cotton. Patterns carry numbers in the forty six hundred series, with pages for each design. A note offers help with colours and stitches from the firm's needlework expert.

The designs are chair backs and arm rests in lacy crochet work. One joins interlocking wedding rings with coloured cloth for a smart effect. The perennial pineapple, a favourite motif, fills another chair back in full. Each pattern lists its thread, size thirty mercerized cotton, and a steel hook. Row by row directions spell out chains, shells, and treble clusters in short forms. A finished back measures about twelve by sixteen inches in size.
69047-the-tiddly-winks:
The Tiddly Winks is a children's book with text by Laura Rountree Smith, issued at Chicago in 1923. Smith wrote other books in the same easy reading line, listed inside the front cover. The pictures are by Haidee Zack Walsh. The book belongs to a series of just right books for young readers.

That series list names open air stories, surprise stories, and tales of twins, among many others. A front picture shows the Tiddly Winks dancing in a ring at a picnic. The plain, large print style of the series suits children reading on their own. Smith's name on the title page links the book to her earlier Tiddly Winks volume, which the series list also names. The whole package is built to be read aloud or alone with ease.
69781-frederick-warne-co-s-list-of-juven:
Frederick Warne and Company's list of juvenile literature, prize books, and gift books for young people is a publisher's catalogue. Its top grade, at seven shillings and sixpence each, is Warne's presentation books. These are square volumes in cloth gilt, with gilt edges and bevelled boards. Hans Andersen's fairy tales head the list, in a complete edition newly translated with sixteen coloured plates.

Grimm's fairy tales follow in the same dress, called a delightful edition of a delightful book. The Arabian Nights entertainments come next, revised with notes and sixteen coloured plates. Robinson Crusoe stands among the same prize volumes. Such lists were bound into books and given to shops and schools. They show what Victorian children were given as prizes for good work. The catalogue preserves the prices, bindings, and review praise with which Warne sold its gift books.
69845-the-club-of-masks:
The Club of Masks is a mystery novel by Allen Upward, copyrighted in 1926. In Britain it appeared as The Domino Club. Burt issued the American edition in New York. The contents run to twenty chapters. His Majesty's service opens the tale in a hush. The narrator slips into a quiet house by the British Museum. A telephone shrills from beside his bed upstairs. He fears to wake the great consultant on his landing.

Evidence from a Madame Bonnell and from the dead follows. An opened safe and a club's books stir the case. The cause of death and an unknown poison are weighed. A cipher's meaning and a finger-print mark the late turns. Upward wrote tales of intrigue with a light hand. Masks and clubs suit his taste for disguise. The novel is a fair specimen of twenties detection.
69980-yanks:
Yanks is a book of soldiers' verse published by G P Putnam's Sons of New York and London in 1919. The poems first appeared in The Stars and Stripes, the official newspaper of the American Expeditionary Forces. The book is dedicated to the children of France.

Privates, sergeants, and captains wrote the pieces, signing name and unit. Hudson Hawley's Just Thinkin' opens the contents. On Learning French and Who Said Sunny France take up the host country. Song of the Censor Man and Beefing handle army grievances in rhyme. The Tank gets its own poem, and Trench Mud gets another. Joyce Kilmer's The Wood Called Rouge-Bouquet stands in the list, marked killed in action. Grantland Rice contributes Song of the Guns. Putnam gathered it as a keepsake of the doughboy's own voice.
70809-jane-austen-and-her-works:
Sarah Tytler wrote this study of Jane Austen and her works for Cassell, with a portrait on steel. Steventon Rectory in Hampshire, Austen's childhood home, is pictured at the front. Tytler's contents run from a life of Austen to chapters on the novels in turn.

Her plan, she says, is to give young people the most characteristic novels with the life in one volume. The tales and the life reflect light on each other, Tytler argues in her preface. 'Pride and Prejudice' gets a long chapter, 'Emma' another, and 'Persuasion' closes the volume, for a generation she calls over-wrought and in some respects over-read.
70935-a-tale-of-three-weeks:
Eglanton Thorne wrote A Tale of Three Weeks for the Religious Tract Society's Little Dot series. Thorne also wrote Kate and her Sister Daisy and Caleb Gaye's Success. Six chapters open with Left Behind. Katie Bartlett comes slowly into the schoolroom where her two younger sisters are setting the tables.

What do you think is going to happen, she asks. Papa and mamma have decided to go away to the seaside. Gertie, eight, and Florrie clap their hands at the splendid news while Katie calls them sillies. Miss Jameson's grand idea, the dolls, a visit to grandmamma, Gertie's birthday, and lessons not learned from books fill the three weeks. Readers get a Victorian children's tale of a household left to itself.
71307-slang-and-cant-in-jerome-k-jerome-:
Slang and Cant in Jerome K. Jerome's Works, a study by Olof Bosson, was published by Heffer in Cambridge in 1911 and printed at Lund. The contents move from a preface and a dated list of Jerome's works to an introduction and a grammatical survey.

The survey has three parts: phonetic notes, accidence, and syntax. Then come the word studies proper: slang, slang passing into colloquial English, vulgarism or cant, and vulgarism passing into colloquial English. The preface states the object: to examine vulgarism and slang in the works of Jerome, born in 1859. Jerome renders the talk of his time with rare accuracy, Bosson argues. His people betray their class and culture in a few words. He had been clerk, teacher, actor, and journalist, and knew many kinds of speech at first hand. The study notes who speaks each expression, and traces its history where it can.
71605-horizons-and-landmarks:
Horizons and Landmarks is a volume of poems by Sidney Royse Lysaght, published by Macmillan at London and New York in 1911. Lysaght had earlier written Poems of the Unknown Way. The contents open with Three Ages of Man, then First Horizons and The Fountain Springs. Our Homeland, Shelter and Fellowship, and The Forest follow.

Later poems treat first love, the world's end, youth, and the quest of youth. The road into the world leads to the country over the hill, and the spirit and the flesh in four parts. Hearth light, the test of faith, a ruined chapel, and hidden paths fill the later pages. The opening poem gives the book its frame: the child is part of all he beholds, youth enfolds the world with dreams of love, and man takes his place as life's guardian. Lysaght writes a reflective, hopeful verse of growth and faith.
72295-the-thames-and-its-docks:
Alexander Forrow of the East and West India Dock Company lectured on The Thames and Its Docks in the winter of 1876-77. He delivered it first at his company's literary institution on December 18, 1876. He gave it again at the City of London College on February 8, 1877. Spottiswoode and Company printed the lecture at London in 1877. Forrow dedicated it to J L du Plat Taylor, his company's secretary.

In his preface Forrow owns the piece was never written for publication. It is a sketch, he says, of a great subject, condensed into a two hours' address. Friends who heard it pressed him to print. He adds some of the rarest plans used to illustrate the talk. The West India Dock's western entrance, with barges waiting to leave, fronts the book.
72338-the-right-side-of-the-tracks:
The Right Side of the Tracks is a science fiction story by Albert Teichner. It appeared in Amazing Stories in May nineteen sixty-three. The setting is a galactic community of ten thousand human planets. Each planet signals all the others once every galactic hour.

Against that law of openness, the planet Nodar has refused to answer for years. The Supreme Council sends the ship Probe, with fifty men, to investigate. Commander Linder is sure the Nodarians are men working up antisocial mischief. Dr Stern, the ship's pessimist, wonders whether they simply want to be left alone. The headnote insists no revolt and no alien capture explains the silence. Something stranger keeps a whole world on its own side of the tracks.
72374-the-emperor-s-candlesticks:
Baroness Emmuska Orczy wrote a novel printed in London in 1899, in twenty two chapters with no heads but numbers. Gay Vienna opens the tale at carnival, on Shrove Tuesday, the last day the church allows for revelry before Lent. Folk had drunk deep of pleasure in bright streets and now take the last drops at the opera ball.

Masks fill the hall, Pierrots and Pierrettes, Fausts and Marguerites, nymphs, fairies, and gnomes chasing in waltz time. In the boxes, black dominoes hide behind half drawn drapes and bright eyes. A richly dressed odalisque whispers to one such domino that she knows who hides under the mask.
74591-george-bernard-shaw-his-life-and-w:
Archibald Henderson's George Bernard Shaw: His Life and Works, an authorized critical biography from Stewart and Kidd of Cincinnati in 1911, carries thirty-three illustrations. Coburn's autochrome portrait fronts the book, and photogravures by Coburn and Steichen are among the plates. The chapters move in order through the life: Dublin days, London, the novelist, the Fabian Society, and Shavian socialism.

Then come the critic years, art, music, and drama in turn, and three chapters on the playwright, followed by the technician, the dramatist, and artist and philosopher. A last chapter, The Man, and a genealogy of the Shaw family close the volume. The illustrations match the text: Fabian tracts, a cartoon by Max Beerbohm, and Shaw at twenty-three and in 1891. Henderson wrote with Shaw's leave and help, and the book is the first full life of a dramatist still very much alive and writing.
7481-the-three-clerks:
Anthony Trollope, born in London in 1815, sets this novel among young men in government offices, the world he knew from his own civil service years. Three clerks, starting together in the lower ranks, face the temptations of Victorian London: ambition, debt, love, and the shortcuts that promise quick success. The introduction suggests the perfect place to read it: under a tree in Kensington Gardens on a summer day.

Trollope follows his clerks through offices, lodgings, and drawing rooms, with the humor and moral sharpness that made him famous. One climbs by talent and luck, another falls by fraud, and the third learns steadiness the hard way. The novel is a young man's guide to getting on, and a warning about what getting on can cost.
74847-tide-marks:
Tomlinson wrote Tide Marks, records of a trip to the beaches of the Moluccas and the forest of Malaya in 1923. Harper printed it at New York in 1924. Kerr Eby drew the pictures. Tomlinson had written The Sea and the Jungle.

The book opens in a London fog so thick that Charing Cross Bridge seems to end midway in space, spanning nothing. Tomlinson reads the dusk as the end of an epoch. Plates then move east: Chinese firemen, Port Said, the Suez Canal, Singapore, and Macassar traders. A front plate shows flames and quiet after a fire. The tone stays elegiac even in the tropics.
74929-the-merivale-banks:
Mary Holmes wrote this novel of a small city's rival banks, published by the Dillingham company at New York under copyrights of 1900 and 1903 and issued in September 1903. Its frontispiece quotes a promise: he has four thousand more we can have. Twenty-four chapters carry the story from The Banks to At Home.

Chapter one sets the scene: two banks stand side by side in one marble-fronted block at Merivale, the First National, called the White Bank, and a private bank called the Grey Bank. Robert White built the block in 1875 and presides over the National, a proud, weak man vain of his year as judge, his general father, and his governor grandfather. His son Herbert opens the family story, with Louie, Fred, a party, a run on the bank, and a crash in the contents.
74955-history-of-the-franks:
Gregory, Bishop of Tours, wrote the great early history of the Franks, here in chosen passages with notes, issued by Columbia University Press in 1916. The book belongs to a series of records of civilization, giving sources in English with guides to their study. Gregory wrote from inside the world he describes.

His history is a chief source for the Frankish kings and the church of his age. The series aimed to put such texts within reach of students who could not read the Latin. Readers get both the bishop's own words and help in placing them. For the early middle ages, few sources carry more weight.
75520-longshanks:
Stephen W Meader wrote Longshanks, held at New York in 1928 with pictures by Edward Shenton. The front print shows a man lifted clear of the ground. Three more prints show a pistol, a beast by a pool, and the print of a bare foot. Tad Hopkins is the boy at the heart of the tale.

Chapter One brings a stage coach down a long hill into Wheeling Town. Long Bill Mifflin drives with a sixteen foot whip. Dusk and chill rise from the river as the coach rolls in. Bill tells Tad of the town's inns, the General Jackson, the Indian Queen, and one more he warns against. Tad has no friends in town but has funds, Bill notes. The tale sets up a river town start for a boy alone.
75723-italian-courtesy-books:
Italian Courtesy-Books, with translations and notes by William Michael Rossetti, was set for the Early English Text Society circle and signed in June 1869. Rossetti says the ask was plain: show what Italy holds in the same line as the manners books of England and France. His claim is bold: thirteenth-century Italy stood as fine in the graces of life as France a century later. The core of the book is Fra Bonvicino da Riva's Fifty Courtesies for the Table, in Italian and English side by side.

Around it stand cuts from Brunetto Latini, Francesco da Barberino, and Agnolo Pandolfini on the rule of a house. Matteo Palmieri speaks on civic life, and the run ends with Castiglione's Courtier and Della Casa's Galateo. Manners fans get the root stock of good form in old verse and prose.
75935-golden-treasury-of-famous-books:
Golden Treasury of Famous Books is Marjory Willison's guide to good reading for boys and girls. The Macmillan Company of Canada published it in Toronto in 1929. Willison arranges the canon in eight parts. Part one treats Dickens, Scott, Shakespeare, and the Bible. Dickens's novels and characters open the guide, with his boyhood and his service to humanity after.

Romance and adventure fill part two. Dumas, Hugo, and Stevenson lead, then Robinson Crusoe and Lorna Doone. Verne, Marryat, Dana, Twain, and Kipling follow. Part three gathers songs of heroes, myths, and fairy tales. Homer, Aesop, Grimm, Andersen, and Malory stand there. Alice in Wonderland and Peter Pan join them. Ballads and verse stories take part four, from Percy's Reliques to Hiawatha. Part five honours Dante, Cervantes, Bunyan, Austen, and the Brontes. History, biography, essays, and poetry complete the course. An afterword and index close the guide.
76070-english-fragments-from-latin-medie:
Henry Littlehales edited these English scraps found inside Latin service books of the Middle Ages. The Early English Text Society issued the book in 1903 as Extra Series ninety. Two coloured facsimiles from old primers face the text.

Littlehales opens with the Manual, the priest's handbook for work outside the church walls. Writs in English hide inside Latin books of hours, mass, and rite, and he prints them here. Notes and headnotes guide the reader through each scrap. Old spellings keep their thorn and yogh letters in this text. Students of early English and of church use alike get raw finds, set in order with care.
76084-the-nowadays-girls-in-the-adironda:
The Nowadays Girls in the Adirondacks is a girls' adventure novel by Gertrude Calvert Hall. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1915. Caswell illustrated the volume for its readers. Its subtitle names the deserted bungalow on Saranac Lake. The contents list thirty five chapters of camp adventure. The Nowadays Club and A Telegram open the tale. Preparations, a missing emerald, and a girl overboard follow. A Night Out, the motor boat, and a dismal prospect raise the stakes.

The mystery deepens around the deserted bungalow in later chapters. Missing, a general alarm, and the search fill the climax. Lost and Found stand as a matched pair near the end. Recovery closes the contents list. Illustrations show the girls dancing, travelling, and finding clues. Sylvia and Hazel are among the girls named in them. The book is a summer camp mystery for girl readers.
77360-american-medicinal-barks:
American Medicinal Barks is a state farm note by Henkel, a help hand in the drug plant work of the plant house. It came out at Washington from the state print house in the year of its issue line. Its chief and staff of the plant house are named at its front.

A note of send from the chiefs room stands there as well. The book serves the new drug plant trade of its day. It tells which barks of the trees and shrubs of America are used in physick. It tells where each grows, how it is got and dried, and how a buyer may know the true bark from the false. Such lore fed a trade that then drew much of its stock from the wild woods.
78066-how-to-write-little-blue-books:
How to Write Little Blue Books is number 1366 of the famous Little Blue Books, the five cent pocket series of Haldeman Julius. Lloyd Smith, an assistant editor of the firm, wrote it at Girard, Kansas, in 1929. By rights the job belonged to the editor himself, Smith says. He is the man who takes or refuses each manuscript, and signs the cheques authors await.

But detail work does not appeal to Haldeman Julius, who prefers to buy from writers who hit his mark at once. So he charged Smith to be plain, full, and very clear. The Little Blue Books had editorial problems of their own, unlike any other series in English. Writers had to fit real knowledge into a tiny pocket book, in simple words, for millions of buyers. This guide tells would be contributors exactly how. It also shows how the cheapest books in America were made.
78280-the-blue-socks:
The Blue Socks, by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, was entered for copyright in 1862 by the American Sunday-School Union. The book adds a plain charge in its second title: Count the Cost. It opens with a girl of about twelve bursting in from school.

Henrietta Laurens begs her mother for money that very minute, to buy yarn for knitting. Her mother sits cutting paper birds for a sick younger child and makes her wait. The plan, once told, is a grand one: a band of girls will each knit socks for a good cause. Chapters on self-denial, progress, and excuses track the work. Elsie's troubles and a tea-party fill the middle, and the close draws the moral home.
78510-how-the-united-states-government-w:
How the United States Government Works is a civics primer by Harry Hibschman, issued as Little Blue Book number 1415 by Haldeman-Julius at Girard, Kansas in 1929. The first chapter owns that government is inescapable: it greets us at birth and leaves us only after our estate is settled. The word itself, the book says, comes through Latin from a Greek word meaning to steer the ship.

Fourteen short chapters follow the machine part by part. Who makes the laws, who carries them out, and who renders justice come first. The President's work, the ways of Congress, the great departments, and the courts follow. Later chapters treat the states, the citizen, the business man, the farmer, and the working man, with a summary at the end.
7871-dutch-fairy-tales-for-young-folks:
William Elliot Griffis's Dutch Fairy Tales for Young Folks opens with a mermaid flying from the sky bearing cheeses. An entangled mermaid, proud of her looks, dwells in a pool half salt and half fresh near the sea. Other tales bring a boy wanting more cheese and a princess with twenty petticoats.

A cat and cradle, Prince Spin Head, a boar with golden bristles, an ice king, elves, and kabouters and bells follow. A woman with 366 children and Santa Klaas with Black Pete close the set. Through Holland's canals and fields, Griffis gives young readers wonder, humor, and a taste of Dutch folk life.
78847-as-a-woman-thinks:
Corra Harris's As a Woman Thinks was published by Houghton Mifflin in 1925, by the author of My Book and Heart. Fifty short chapters hold her thoughts on a life, from When I Was a Child to Can We Be Happy. Early pieces treat her father and mother, her mother's God, book learning, and school days. A year in Oxford gets its own chapter. Later pieces take up love and authorship, the mind of the writer, and advice to those who want to write.

The opening chapter refuses mysticism at once: no aura, no oversoul, no phonographing of the immortal part. Her mind, she says, was laid off by the latitudes and longitudes of actual experience. War, widowhood, reputation, and various types of women fill the middle of the book. Garden happiness, the country and the town, and why worship Europe close the sequence.
79362-mavericks:
W C Tuttle wrote a western novel whose contents open with the crime. Murder or self defense asks the second chapter. A strange quest and a hard luck stranger follow. Bill McGill finds two friends by chapter five. Hashknife gets down to work in chapter six, and Bill follows his nose in the seventh.

Hashknife and Sleepy hire out, ghosts appear, and murder returns by chapter ten. Caliente and Piute throw a party. The brand venters and a journey to Santa Dolores build the end. Chapter one sets the scene years ago, in a dilapidated shack near a brushy mesa by the Painted Desert. Tuttle's Hashknife Hartley was a beloved range detective.
79623-neptune-speaks:
Frank Richardson Pierce wrote a sea tale told by an old shipwright called peculiar by his fishing village. Gossiping wives said he was a little off, the narrator begins. Too old to lay keels in the shipyard, he retired to a beachcomber's shack. There he watched ships pass whose keels he had supervised. The narrator was present when the Aleut's keel was laid.

She was his last ship, lost with all hands after striking a rock on her maiden voyage. The mystery of her sinking worried him. The great tragedies of the sea are never told, he often said, because no one survives. Pierce frames the tale as Neptune speaking through the old man.
79706-arithmetical-books:
Arithmetical Books is a bibliography by Augustus De Morgan, professor of mathematics in University College, London, published by Taylor and Walton in 1847. Its full title promises brief notices of a large number of works, drawn up from actual inspection. The books listed run from the invention of printing to De Morgan's own time.

De Morgan dedicates the work to George Peacock, dean of Ely. A motto from the Dublin Review makes the case for such lists. A compiler's catalogue, the reviewer says, may two centuries later be the only authority on several points. De Morgan examined the books himself rather than copying other lists. The result remains a foundation for the history of arithmetic teaching. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
79716-women-s-barracks:
Tereska Torres wrote of her years with Free French women in war, first issued in 1950. Fawcett Publications brought out Women's Barracks in New York that year. George Cummings, who knew Torres in wartime London, wrote a translator's preface. He met her circle at a Down Street mansion turned into barracks.

Torres was seventeen, a convent schoolgirl near Orleans, when war began. Her father, a sculptor, enlisted as France fell into the phony war. She joined the women's division of the Free French Forces in London. The book tells, with tenderness, how shared barracks life changed young women.
818-the-aeroplane-speaks:
H. Barber, a captain in the Royal Flying Corps, wrote this guide to help the ordinary reader grasp the aeroplane and the pilot's life. He states two aims: to explain the machine and its joys and troubles, and to offer something of practical use. The book is his first effort as an author, written from flying experience.

Barber describes controls, engines, wind, and the feel of flight in plain terms, with the pilot's view to the fore. He writes for the curious layman, not the engineer, and his tone is eager and direct. The book is a lively record of early military flying, when the aeroplane was still a wonder and a risk.
8220-remarks:
Bill Nye, Edgar W. Nye, published Remarks with over one hundred and fifty illustrations by J. H. Smith, opening with verses by Bret Harte on Ah Sin. Nye's directions explain the book's plan: it is not designed for any one class, but is a universal repository of thought, containing some of his best thoughts. Though omitting any thought he judged better left unthought, which is why the book is not so large as intended. The humour that follows is deadpan, self-mocking, and American.

Nye was one of the most popular humorists of the Gilded Age, and Remarks shows why: short pieces, jokes, and observations on everyday life, delivered with a wink. The illustrations add to the fun. For readers of American humour, the volume is a classic of its kind, and a reminder of how the West laughed at itself.
855-clocks:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short piece on clocks, in the comic, reflective vein of his best essays. He muses on the tyranny of timepieces, on clocks that gain, lose, or stop, and on the human habit of watching the hands while life slips by. The transcriber's note keeps his old spellings, such as to-night and to-morrow.

Jerome's humour is gentle and domestic, turning a household object into a mirror of our fuss and folly. The piece is brief, but it shows his gift for finding philosophy in the everyday. It suits readers who like a light essay that makes them smile at their own watch, and then think twice about it.
8592-poetical-works:
George Gilfillan edited this volume of the poetical works of Charles Churchill, the eighteenth-century satirist, with a memoir, critical essay, and explanatory notes. Gilfillan opens by placing Churchill among writers who, in Goldsmith's phrase, narrowed great gifts to party ends: a man who might have been poet, hero, or saint. Became a fierce satirist, an unlucky politician, and a profligate who died young.

The poems themselves attack the politics, theatre, and society of Georgian London with speed and bite, naming names and sparing no one. Gilfillan's notes help modern readers follow jokes aimed at long-dead targets. The book suits readers of Augustan satire who want Churchill entire. A Victorian editor's sympathetic but frank life of a talent that burned fast and left a sharp mark.
8899-three-weeks:
Elinor Glyn introduces Three Weeks to American readers in 1907, answering misunderstanding and misrepresentation from nearly the entire English press and a section of the public. For her, the Lady of the novel was a deep study, the analysis of a strange Slav nature who, from circumstances, education. Her general view of life, stood beyond ordinary laws of morality. If she were studying a tiger, Glyn says, she would not give it a spaniel's attributes because the public might prefer a spaniel. She would portray it accurately, even so.

The novel itself follows an Englishman and an older, married Slav noblewoman through three weeks of passionate love in Switzerland and Venice, ending in tragedy. Glyn's frank treatment of female desire made the book notorious and bestselling. Readers today meet a key text of early twentieth-century popular romance.
941-just-folks:
Edgar A. Guest wrote these homely poems for just folks, dedicated to the little mother and the memory of the big father. The title poem speaks of queer folks who talk of weather and good times. Roses budding and bees on nectar sprees appear, with the scarlet fever scare and other small trials of family life woven in.

Guest's verse is plain, rhymed, and sentimental, praising home, work, and neighbourly kindness. He was the people's poet of his day, read aloud at kitchen tables across America. The book charms readers who like simple, heartfelt verse, where everyday life is treated as worthy of song.
9567-narrative-and-legendary-poems-compl:
Volume one of Whittier's works holds his complete Narrative and Legendary Poems, revised with his own notes. The book opens with The Vaudois Teacher, The Female Martyr, and The Funeral Tree of the Sokokis, then runs through Cassandra Southwick, The Bridal of Pennacook, and Barclay of Ury. Skipper Ireson's Ride, The Sycamores, and Telling the Bees follow. Each poem carries head-notes on its source and date.

Later poems in the volume span Among the Hills, Mabel Martin, and The Pennsylvania Pilgrim, with tales of faith, exile, and home. Whittier's voice stays plain and earnest throughout. A reader gets the full narrative Whittier in one volume, and the best start for his storytelling verse.
addresses-by-the-right-reverend-phillips: Phillips Brooks, bishop of Massachusetts, delivers these addresses, published at Philadelphia in 1895 by Henry Altemus. The contents run from The Beauty of a Life of Service and Thought and Action through The Duty of the Christian Business Man and True Liberty. The Christ in Whom Christians Believe and Abraham Lincoln close the volume. The opening address takes the words of Jesus from the eighth chapter of Saint John, that the truth shall make you free. It asks the purpose and result of that freedom.
adventures-among-books:
Andrew Lang ranges across his reading life in essays first printed in magazines, as his preface records, this text following the 1912 Longmans edition. Recollections of Robert Louis Stevenson stand near the front, written by a friend who shared Stevenson's tastes. Other chapters treat Oliver Wendell Holmes, William Morris's poems, and Mrs. Radcliffe's novels.

Lang writes on Smollett, Hawthorne, Saint Augustine's Confessions, the supernatural in fiction, and the art of storytelling itself. A final essay, The Paradise of Poets, looks at where poets rank the dead. The book is a scholar-poet's commonplace shelf, learned without heaviness, and it invites readers to wander their own libraries.
among-famous-books: John Kelman lectures among famous books, guiding readers through great works with a minister's warmth and a critic's eye. The lectures open on the pleasures and duties of reading, then turn to individual books and authors. Kelman's aim is not scholarship alone but friendship with books, and the habit of reading well.
b09-luther-good-works:
Martin Luther wrote A Treatise on Good Works in 1520 to answer a plain question: if faith alone saves, what should a Christian do? His answer walks through the Ten Commandments one by one. Each command becomes a guide to the shape of a faithful life at home, at work, and in prayer.

Luther teaches that a work is good because faith makes the worker right, not the other way around. The first command, trust in God, anchors all the rest. The treatise is his fullest work on daily morals from those years. It shows the Reformation speaking to kitchens and workshops, not only to scholars.
black-rock-a-tale-of-the-selkirks:
Black Rock, a novel by Ralph Connor, tells of a mining and lumber settlement in the Selkirk Mountains of western Canada. Connor knew that frontier world from his own missionary work there, and an introduction by George Adam Smith stresses that firsthand knowledge. A young minister, Mr. Craig, arrives among rough camps where drink and gambling do heavy damage.

Christmas Eve in a lumber camp opens the tale, followed by a saloon fight the men call their Waterloo. Mrs. Mavor's story deepens the human cost of camp life. Craig and his allies form a league against drink, hold a first communion, and watch their pact strain and break. Connor mixes adventure, humor, and open Christian appeal in a portrait of men fighting for cleaner lives.
britannica-1911-algae-occurrence-in-the-:
Occurrence in the Rocks, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, asks why so few algae survive as fossils. Soft algal tissue rots away, so preservation is rare except where the body is hardened with silica, as in the diatoms, or with carbonate of lime, as in the coralline algae. The section calls the poor record unsurprising on that ground alone.

Yet descent makes the puzzle pointed, since mosses and vascular plants are believed to spring from algal ancestors, implying an age of algae before the Carboniferous forests. Many Silurian and Devonian remains once described as algae rest on evidence now judged inadequate. Calcareous Siphonales are well represented from the Silurian to the Tertiary, while diatoms appear only from the chalk onward. The Devonian fossil Nematophycus is believed to be a kelp-like alga. Fossil algae grow frequent only in late Secondary and Tertiary formations.
britannica-1911-banker-marks:
Banker-marks, also called masons' marks, are explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A banker is the stone bench on which a mason works his blocks. The article argues that banker-marks is the better name for the signs cut on stones. The setters who place the stones, chosen from the best workmen, cut no marks themselves.

Such marks are found on old buildings of note all over the civilized world. One scholar quoted found the same careful masonry and tool marks across four lands. In England, France, Sicily, and Palestine the work of the twelfth century matched. Later marks were made with a toothed chisel, but the aim stayed the same. Each mark tied a single craftsman to his own work beyond dispute. Simple designs recur often, since few shapes are easy to cut. Now and then a mark of very fancy form turns up among them.
britannica-1911-barracks:
Barracks are the buildings that house military or naval forces. They hold quarters for officers, warrant officers, non-commissioned officers, and men. They also hold messes and recreation rooms, regimental offices, shops, stores, stables, and vehicle sheds. The word came through French from a late Latin term for a bar. It usually names permanent brick or stone buildings for troops in peacetime.

Hut barracks of corrugated iron lined with wood also count, built near training grounds with somewhat less room, closer to camp conditions. The 1911 Britannica entry, a very long one, works chiefly through the British system. Accommodation follows the Barrack Synopsis, an official schedule. It lays down, item by item, the buildings and fittings each unit is authorized to have. Its rules come from decisions made by authority over time.
britannica-1911-caudine-forks:
Caudine Forks, a pass in Samnium, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Latin name is Furculae Caudinae. The pass is famous for a disaster that struck the Roman army there. That befell in the second Samnite War, in the year 321 BC.

Livy pictures two narrow, wooded gorges with a plain between them. The plain was grassy and well watered, but ringed wholly by mountains. A road, later the Appian Way, ran through that trap. The Romans marched in unopposed, bound to relieve a friendly town. They found the exit blocked by the enemy in force. Turning back, they saw the entrance and the hills also held against them. There was no way of escape for the trapped army. The article then weighs which modern plain fits Livy's tale. A plain west of Caudium is judged the only site that suits an army of forty thousand.
britannica-1911-ember-days-and-ember-wee:
Ember Days and Ember Weeks are the four seasons set apart by the Western Church for special prayer and fasting, and for the ordaining of clergy. In the medieval Church they were called quatuor tempora. The Ember weeks follow Holy Cross day on 14 September, St Lucy's day on 13 December, the first Sunday in Lent, and Whitsun day.

The entry weighs two roots for the word, from the Anglo-Saxon ymb-ren, a circuit, or from the Latin quatuor tempora by way of German quatember. The rite is confined to the Western Church and began as a church ordinance in Rome. The fasts likely began as preparation for Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost, with a fourth added for balance with the four seasons. In Leo the Great's time, from 440 to 461, the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday pattern was already fixed. From Rome the days spread slowly through Western Christendom.
britannica-1911-gilyaks: Gilyaks are a mixed people of the lower Amur region in the far east. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says they once spread widely there but now live in the Amur delta and north Sakhalin. Some scholars link them to the Ainu, but the entry favors mixed roots. Two physical types are described from field study of the group. Chinese call them fish skin clad people, from salmon skin dress. A list of studies on Amur peoples closes the short entry.
britannica-1911-greenbacks:
Greenbacks were a form of United States paper currency, named for the green colour on the backs of the notes. The 1911 Britannica entry calls them treasury notes, first issued in 1862 as a question of hard necessity, to pay for the Civil War. With specie payment suspended, they were an inconvertible currency made legal tender: fiat money.
