Three acts, in February and July 1862 and March 1863, each authorized 150 million dollars of notes. They fell hard, at the lowest to 35 cents on the dollar. A retirement plan begun in 1866 was halted in 1868. Specie payment resumed on 1 January 1879, with 346,681,000 dollars of notes outstanding, a figure the entry says still stands. It then treats the Greenback party, which first ran a presidential candidate, Peter Cooper, in 1876.
britannica-1911-kumyks:
The Kumyks are a people of Turkish stock in Caucasia. They hold the Kumyk plateau in north Daghestan and south Terek, and the lands along the Caspian shore. Some see in them the Kami and Kamaks known to Ptolemy. Others take them for descendants of the Khazars. Vambéry holds that they settled in their present home in the 8th century, in the great days of the Khazar kingdom. Some Kabardians also settled there later. The Russians built forts in their land in 1559 and again under Peter the Great.

The Kumyks have long been more settled in their ways than the mountain peoples around them, and have held some respect among them for it. They farm the upper terraces of their plateau, which are very fertile. The lower ground they leave to the Nogai Tatars.
britannica-1911-mckees-rocks: McKees Rocks is a borough of Allegheny County in Pennsylvania, set out in a short 1911 Britannica place note. It stands on the Ohio River a few miles north west of Pittsburg. Its folk grew fast to fourteen thousand seven hundred two by nineteen ten. Two rail lines serve the borough for freight. Soft coal and gas lie in the ground close at hand. Coal and wood ship out, and shops make goods of many kinds. First homes rose in eighteen thirty, and borough form came in eighteen ninety two.
britannica-1911-meshcheryaks:
Meshcheryaks, a people of eastern Russia, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The chronicler Nestor held them to be Finns, and part of a kindred people still call themselves by their name. Another scholar took them for a mix of Finns and Turks. A Hungarian traveller found that the Tatar branch of them on the Obi closely matched Hungarians.

The article says they once held the basin of the Oka river and land reaching north-east to the Volga. After Russia conquered the Kazan empire, part of them moved north-east to other river basins. The people thus split in two. The western branch took on the customs, tongue, and faith of the Russians. The eastern branch took on those of the Bashkirs, with whom it was merging when the entry was written.
britannica-1911-rudolph-king-of-the-fran:
Rudolph, king of the Franks, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was also called Raoul. He died in 936. He was duke of Burgundy before he was king. His father was Richard, duke of Burgundy. He was most likely a member of the Carolingian family.

He became duke of Burgundy on his father's death in 921. He married Emma, daughter of Robert, duke of the Franks. He helped his father-in-law drive Charles the Simple from his throne. Robert then became king of the Franks. When Robert was killed in battle in June 923, Rudolph succeeded him. He was crowned at Soissons in the following month. He gave Burgundy to his brother-in-law, Giselbert of Vergi. The new king was fully occupied from then on. He fought off the attacks of the Normans. He also combated the partisans of Charles the Simple.
britannica-1911-sevenoaks:
Sevenoaks, a market town in Kent, England, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 22 miles south-east of London on the South-Eastern and Chatham railway. Its urban district held 8,106 people in 1901. The town sits prettily on high ground among the wooded North Downs. Below it runs the valley of the river Darent.

Two main streets meet at the south end of the town, near the church of St Nicholas. That church holds monuments of the Amherst family and a tablet to William Lambarde. Lambarde wrote the Perambulation of Kent and founded a college for the poor at Greenwich. The grammar school dates from 1418, founded by Sir William Sevenoke. He also founded almshouses tied to the school. Close by stands Knole Park, one of the finest old houses in England.
britannica-1911-slovaks:
Slovaks are a Slav people of some two and a half million souls. The 1911 Britannica entry places most of them in the north of Hungary. To the west they reach into Lower Austria and into Moravia. The river Morava and the Jablunka hills mark that west edge. To the north they touch the Poles on the Silesian frontier.

On the east they meet the Little Russians on a bent line. On the south the Magyars are their neighbours from Pressburg east. Within those bounds they live much unmixed, save in the towns. Their chief centre is St Marton on the Turocz, the entry says. They seem to have held this land since the 400s or 500s.
britannica-1911-ticks:
Ticks is a zoology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ticks are the common name for creatures of the mite order, forming two families named in Latin in the entry. Together they can be told from other mites by a central probe under the mouth. That probe is armed with teeth that curve backward.

Ticks are large for their kind, the article notes. A swollen female of some species can measure half an inch or more in length. Even the newly hatched young are hardly tiny enough to need a microscope. The skin is tough, leathery, or horny. The mouth parts hold two small jaws that can draw back, a pair of short feelers, and the toothed probe. All of these sit on a movable horny plate.
britannica-1911-tilbury-docks:
Tilbury Docks on the Thames in Essex get a short port entry in the 1911 Britannica. The docks lie across from Gravesend, down stream from London Bridge. They count as part of the Port of London. A dock firm built them in eighteen eighty six. Four docks plus a tidal basin and locks cover seventy four acres in all. Water in the basin runs deep at high tide and holds depth at low tide.

Long quays and large sheds serve ships and freight at the site. The great passenger steamers for London tie up here. Rail links run to the town line for Tilbury and to goods lines in the north. Folk get rooms and help at the port as well.
britannica-1911-turks:
Turks is a word used in three senses, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article sets them apart. In the political sense, a Turk is a Muslim subject of the sultan of Turkey. The term is not properly used of Christians in the East. Its use for Arabs, Albanians, or Kurds in Turkey is common but, the article says, hardly correct.

The linguistic sense is the most satisfactory, the article argues. It names a well-marked division of the Ural-Altaic languages and their speakers. Most people called Turks have spoken them since the sixth century. The racial sense is harder, since Turks are hard to set apart by build or custom from kindred peoples. Today, the article says, Turks are Muslim speakers of Turkish tongues in western Asia.
britannica-1911-uskoks:
Uskoks were folk who fled their homes as Turks took Bosnia and lands near it in the early part of the fifteen hundreds. Their name comes from a word that means one who has fled. They first held a fort near Spalato and warred on the Turks from there. When that post failed, they moved to Zengg on the Croat shore.

Austria took them in as guards of the march lands and pledged gold each year. The gold came late or not at all, so they turned to sea raids. Their swift boats hid in small creeks and struck trade ships in the gulf. Venice then bore the brunt of their raids.
by-berwen-banks:
Allen Raine wrote a Welsh novel, By Berwen Banks, in a print past its one hundred eleventh thousand. Hutchinson of London put out the book. Raine had won her name with A Welsh Singer and Torn Sails. Twenty-one chapters line the frame. Caer Madoc, a sleepy Welsh town two miles from the sea, opens the tale.

The town holds itself next to London in worth, its folk hold, with church, three chapels, and a mayor. The house on the cliff and a chapel meet come next. Storm, and the coming of Gwynne Ellis, turn the run. Corwen and Valmai give the love thread its names. An old register, a fate web, and a black dog mark the dark mid-run. Babies' corner, unrest, and the Merediths lead home again at the close. Welsh shore, chapel, and kin form the ground.
cape-cod-folks:
Sarah P. McLean Greene wrote tales of Cape Cod folk, first lodged in 1881 and again in 1904. Grosset and Dunlap put out this copy at New York. Plates come from the stage play of the book. Wallencamp, its town, fills the frame. A school teacher from off-Cape tells the tales, by the first heads' hints.

On a mission and a horn blown open the set. Wallencamp beaux do a grave deed in the third. A turkey mogul lands in the fourth. Grandma Keeler gets Grandpa set for Sunday school in the fifth. Becky and the Cradlebows, a kiss in class, and fun at the Ark fill the heart. Lovell Barlow pops the ask in the ninth. A fisherman's letter, a fun'ral, and Becky's own tale of fault mark the turns. Cape speech and Cape ways form the stock.
captains-courageous-a-story-of-the-grand:
Rudyard Kipling sent a spoiled rich boy to sea school in Captains Courageous, his novel of the Grand Banks cod fleet. Harvey Cheyne, fifteen, son of a railroad millionaire, washes off a liner in the North Atlantic fog. A fishing schooner picks him up, and Captain Disko Troop refuses his money and puts him to work beside the captain's son Dan.

Harvey baits lines, cleans fish, stands watch, and learns the whole hard economy of the Banks through one season. Kipling fills the decks with dialect, weather, gear, and men's talk, drawn from real Gloucester fishermen. The boy who returns to his parents has been remade by wages and work. It remains the great boys' book of the fishing fleets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-candles:
An altar candlestick has five parts: foot, stem, knob at mid-stem, bowl catching wax drippings, and pricket, the sharp point holding the candle. A spring tube holding a small candle may replace the pricket. Early lights hung from ceilings or walls or stood on pedestals, fed with oil as canthari or holding candles as phari.

No evidence puts candlesticks on the altar before the tenth century, and Leo IV allowed only saints' relics and the Gospel book there. Acolytes carried candlesticks set on the sanctuary floor, as Eastern churches still do. By the thirteenth century Durandus describes a candlestick at each altar corner, and the custom became general in the sixteenth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arawaks:
The Arawaks, also called Aruacans, were the first American native peoples met by Columbus, not to be confused with the Aroacas, linguistically allied to the Chibchas of Colombia. Arawak-speaking tribes spread widely over South America, from the Paraguay sources to Lake Maracaibo's northwestern shores. They also spread from the eastern Andes slopes of Peru and Bolivia to the Atlantic coast of Guyana. Columbus met them in 1492 in the Bahamas, then in Haiti, Cuba, Jamaica, and Puerto Rico.

That century, and perhaps for centuries before, Arawak peoples held the Greater Antilles, and may once have held every West Indian island. Then Caribs, pressing from the Venezuelan mainland, gradually took the southern Antilles and drove Arawaks northward, who feared their aggressors. The entry maps a language family across a continent and an island world remade by invasion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candlesticks:
Little is known of the earliest candlesticks in Christian churches. Constantine's gifts to the Lateran and Saint Peter's seem mostly stands and hanging chandeliers for lamps. They include two sets of seven bronze candelabra ten feet high before the altars, though those may not have held wax tapers. Great hanging crowns of gold and silver, bearing fifty, eighty, or 120 little dolphin branches each holding lamps, lit the great feasts.

Rohault de Fleury counts 8,730 lights that Constantine destined for the Lateran basilica, and such crowns lasted through the Middle Ages across East and West. Besides these, plain candlesticks were surely in use from very early times, and the seven candlesticks of the Apocalypse likely mirror a feature already familiar in worship. Smaller survivors, like a bronze chandelier shaped as a basilica holding a dozen lights, show how these works were built.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-censorship-of:
Censorship of books is the supervision of the press to prevent abuse of it. Every lawful authority charged with shielding its subjects from a pernicious press has the right to exercise it. Censorship falls into two kinds, ecclesiastical and civil, depending on whether a spiritual or secular authority practices it. It works in two ways: before printing or publication, by examining a work, and after printing or publication, by repressing or prohibiting it.

The classical word censura covers both meanings, especially in Roman Church legislation. In later civil law it came to mean almost only examination beforehand. Wherever past centuries speak of abolishing censorship, only the prior kind is meant. Freedom of the press, the reverse of censorship, is nowhere unlimited. Abuse may be condemned and punished under common law, and old censorship has nearly everywhere given way to stricter press laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chinooks:
An entry on the Chinooks, an Indian people of the lower Columbia River from the Dalles to its mouth. Divided into Lower and Upper Chinooks, they lived in large wooden houses holding several families, grouped into villages on the north bank of the Columbia and Willamette, each under an independent chief. Their staple food was salmon with roots and berries, and they were great traders, carrying goods in high-prowed canoes as far as Nootka Sound.

Contact with whites brought a trade jargon of Chinook and Nootkan words, later widened by other tongues, and it brought ruin as well. The entry presents the tribe as an example of civilisation unprepared by religion, thinned by vice and disease until the Lower Chinooks died out. Missionary visits by Father Demers in 1840 baptised children but won few lasting converts, and today no more than 300 Chinooks remain, mostly on reservations in Oregon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creeks:
An ethnological entry describes the Creeks, an important confederacy of Indian tribes and remnants, chiefly of Muskogian stock. They once held most of Georgia and Alabama's central and southern lands, but now live in eastern Oklahoma. Their name first belonged to their homeland, the Creek Country, not to the people.

The dominant tribe is the Maskoki, about half the whole body, alongside Hichitee, Koasati, and Yuchi, each with its own language. The Seminole began as a separated band of Creeks. In the colonial period the Creeks held the balance between English Carolina and Spanish and French Florida and Louisiana. Their English alliance helped destroy the Franciscan missions of upper Florida in 1702 to 1708, carrying off 1,400 mission Indians as slaves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-index-of-proh:
Once the Church's official list of books Catholics were forbidden to read, the Index is explained here as part of a larger code of book law. The list itself was the second and larger half of a volume called the Index librorum prohibitorum, which gathered all church legislation about books. A separate article on book censorship covers the wider system behind it.

Books reached the list by decree of a Roman congregation, such as the Holy Office or the Congregation of the Index, with papal approval in common form. The pope could also act alone by bull or brief. The entry explains that process. Complaints led to a book being examined. A listing then shaped what Catholic readers could read.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-italo-greeks:
Greeks in Italy who keep the Byzantine rite are the Italo-Greeks of this entry, sorted into three classes. First, church communities that have followed the Greek rite since Byzantine days; second, Greek colonies in port cities and at Rome. Third, descendants of Greeks and Albanians who fled the Turkish conquest of the Balkans in mass migration to southern Italy, founding towns and strong local groups.

That third group long kept its own tongue and customs and still keeps the Greek rite, though in other ways it has merged into Italian life. Whether any southern Italian or Sicilian diocese used the Greek rite before the eighth century is hard to say. Gradual hellenization and many Greek monasteries surely shaped liturgical life. The entry maps a rite surviving across conquest, migration, and absorption.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-bo:
Liturgical books are the official volumes that hold the texts and rubrics, the directions, for a church's public worship. They are the yardstick for what counts as liturgical: a rite is official only if it stands in one of these books, a point the entry stresses against private devotion books.

Early Christians had no such volumes beyond the Bible, since forms lived in memory and habit. This long survey traces how fixed prayers came to be written down, then gathered into the Missal, Breviary, and kin. Roman books come first, followed by shorter accounts of the books of other rites, East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayer-books:
By prayer books, usage means a store of prayer forms meant for private devotion, set apart from service books, which hold the set forms of public worship. The early Christian centuries left no such book, and we cannot be sure any then stood. Bishop Serapion's Prayer book, is more a Pontifical than a prayer book, and was surely not meant for private use.

Later prayer books swelled with high claims. A prayer said ere a picture of Christ crucified bore, by a supposed grant of Gregory III, as many days of indulgence as wounds in the Saviour's Body. A supposed grant of Boniface VIII speaks of eighty thousand years. In truth no curb on print stood in the early sixteenth century. The Congregation of the Index came only after the Council of Trent, so ere Trent booksellers were free to print near any wild claim that might help sales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raskolniks:
Raskolniks, from the Russian raskol, schism or splitting, is a general name for dissidents from the Established Church in Russia. This encyclopedia entry groups under it the many offshoots of the Greek Orthodox Church of the Russian Empire, as Russian historians and church writers use the term. Strictly, the name covers only those who kept the outward forms of the Byzantine Rite. Others, who dropped its ritual as well as its teaching, fall under sectarianism instead.

The entry treats both kinds together, since either form of dissent is little known outside Russia. It compares the Raskolniks to an antithesis of Protestantism against Catholicism within Russian Orthodoxy. Later splits produced the Encyclicalists, who backed the tsar and agreed with the Established Church on main points, and the Controversialists, who denied those points. A third group, the Yedinovertsi or Uniates, entered union with the Established Church while keeping all their peculiar practices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silvester-jen:
Silvester Jenks, theologian born in Shropshire about 1656, died in December 1714. He was schooled at Douai College, where he taught philosophy from 1680 to 1686. He later preached in ordinary to James II. The Revolution of 1688 sent him fleeing to Flanders. Returning to England, he labored as a missionary in or near London and was named Archdeacon of Surrey and Kent by the chapter.

In 1711 Propaganda elected him Vicar Apostolic of the Northern District, but he died of paralysis before consecration. His works include A Contrite and Humble Heart of 1692 and Practical Discourses on the Morality of the Gospel of 1699. Later came The Whole Duty of a Christian of 1707 and A Short Review of the Book of Jansenius of 1710.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-franks:
Germanic tribes banded along the Rhine's right bank, from Mainz to the sea, form the confederation at the centre of this entry. Roman writers first name the Franks in a battle of about 241. In the third century some crossed into Belgic Gaul along the Meuse and Scheldt, and Rome, after failed efforts to expel them, settled for alliance.

Julian's victory in 359 did not destroy them, and the Franks of Belgium turned peaceful settlers, even backing Rome against the invasion of 406. Clovis, conversion, and the Merovingian kingdom carry the tale forward, with law, church life, and the slow making of France. It is a full account of a people who outlasted the empire they served.
clocks:
Jerome K Jerome opens Clocks by dividing the species in two: the clock that is always wrong and glories in it, and the clock that is right until you rely on it. From that distinction he spins a short comic essay on household timepieces, church clocks, and human self-deception. Appearance, he suggests, is a king who must be kept up at great effort.

Jerome treats clocks as characters with morals, praising honest wrongness over respectable fraud. The Lord-of-Lies passage in the middle shows his satire widening from mantelpieces to all mankind bowing before King Appearances. The piece is brief, genial, and exact, a good taste of the humor that made Jerome famous well beyond Three Men in a Boat.
complete-poetical-works:
Bret Harte's Complete Poetical Works gathers the verse of the Argonaut Edition, opening with a biographical sketch of the California writer. The sketch follows Harte from Albany to California in 1854, through jobs as miner, teacher, express messenger, and printer, to the editorship of the Overland Monthly. Poems are grouped as national pieces, Spanish idyls and legends, dialect verse, and miscellaneous poems.

Here are John Burns of Gettysburg, the mission legends of Padre Junípero, and Dickens in Camp. The dialect section holds Plain Language from Truthful James, the famous Heathen Chinee poem, with The Society upon the Stanislaus and other mining-camp ballads. Harte's poems made him famous beside his tales; this volume shows their full range, from Civil War sentiment to frontier comedy.
complete-project-gutenberg-john-galswort:
John Galsworthy's works are gathered in this collected volume, and the contents open with the Forsyte books in their order. The Man of Property stands as the first volume of the saga, followed by the interlude Indian Summer of a Forsyte and In Chancery; Awakening and To Let complete the third volume. The chronicle of the Forsyte family's property instinct is the spine of the set.

The other novels are shelved beside it: The Dark Flower, The Freelands, Beyond, Saint's Progress, The Island Pharisees, The Country House, Fraternity, and The Patrician. Villa Rubein and Other Stories and Five Short Tales hold the shorter fiction, including The Apple Tree and The First and Last. Essays and studies, from the Inn of Tranquility pieces to Quality, close the collection. It is a working library of Galsworthy between two covers.
complete-project-gutenberg-oliver-wendel:
Oliver Wendell Holmes's writings are gathered here in one collected volume, and the contents read as the map of a double career. The breakfast-table books come first: The Autocrat, The Professor, and The Poet at the Breakfast Table, with Over the Teacups to close the series. Those table-talk volumes made him famous on two continents.

The novels follow: Elsie Venner, The Guardian Angel, and A Mortal Antipathy. Pages from an Old Volume of Life gathers essays. The Medical Essays give the other Holmes, the Harvard anatomist who argued the contagiousness of puerperal fever before the profession would hear it. Memoirs of Motley and of Emerson, and Our Hundred Days in Europe, complete the list. Poet, novelist, and physician speak in one volume here, in the order his readers knew them.
complete-project-gutenberg-william-dean-:
William Dean Howells is gathered here in a large Project Gutenberg compilation of his writings, assembled by David Widger and other contributors. Howells, the Ohio-born editor and novelist, shaped American realism for decades. The file sorts his output into three groups: studies, novels, and plays. New pieces were meant to be added as volunteers produced them.

Studies include Literary Friends and Acquaintance, essays on Henry James and Emile Zola, and the piece on the man of letters as a man of business. Novels run from The Rise of Silas Lapham to Dr Breen's Practice and Fennel and Rue. Short plays such as The Sleeping-Car and The Elevator close the set. Readers can sample a whole career in one place, moving between criticism, fiction, and farce.
doe-osti-3577306-control-room-of-the-fut:
Argonne report ANL-26/42 recaps a workshop on the control room of the future testbed. Ashley M. Yates, Caitlyn Sarna, and Duane R. Verner are among the authors. Control rooms for reactors and grids face aging screens and new AI tools at once.

Participants said trust is not the only barrier to new tools. Operators resist opening yet another application with its own interface. Tools in use for years or decades feel safer by habit. Explainable AI may build trust by showing its reasoning. Testbed planners learn to design for operator habits, not just new features.
dutch-fairy-tales-for-young-folks:
William Elliot Griffis, a lifelong student of Holland, retells Dutch folk tales for children in Dutch Fairy Tales for Young Folks. Twenty-one tales fill the contents, from The Entangled Mermaid to Why the Stork Loves Holland. The first tale gives a young mermaid in a pool half salt and half fresh, near a river mouth, whose gray-bearded father owns the island where the mermaids picnic.

Cheese runs through the book like a national joke: one boy wants more cheese, and a frontispiece shows cheeses flying out of the sky. The princess with twenty petticoats, the cat and the cradle, Brabo and the giant, and Santa Klaas with Black Pete carry Dutch legend and custom to young readers. Griffis keeps the tone bright and the morals light, and the tales double as a first tour of Holland's dikes, towns, and sea fights.
familiar-studies-of-men-and-books:
Robert Louis Stevenson collected these magazine essays as Familiar Studies of Men and Books, studies first printed in the Cornhill and other journals. The contents move from Victor Hugo's romances and Robert Burns to Walt Whitman, Henry David Thoreau, and Samuel Pepys. An eleventh edition appeared in 1896, testimony to steady demand.

Stevenson also profiles the Japanese reformer Yoshida Torajiro, the poet-thief Francois Villon, Charles of Orleans, and John Knox's dealings with women. He writes as a fellow craftsman, judging style and character together, generous to oddity and allergic to cant. The Burns and Whitman essays especially show the young Stevenson thinking hard about what makes a writer live.
five-happy-weeks:
Sangster tells of a parting in Five Happy Weeks, a tale for children entered in 1875. Margaret Elizabeth Munson Sangster sets her story in a home where the mother is ill. The doctor says a five weeks' rest away is the only thing that will restore her health. She cannot bear to leave the children, and her husband must go with her.

Edith, Mabel, and Johnnie are left to Aunt Maria. The sampled pages show the children's own test of her. They make what Johnnie calls a Bible feast, for the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind. Aunt Maria owns that she had only tried them a little, and begs their pardon. Sangster's tale teaches duty and kindness inside one family's five weeks of trial.
from-the-ranks:
King opens this army novel with a shot in the night. A sentry on post Number Five fired at someone unknown. The officer of the day ordered the shot and now stays silent. By morning the whole garrison buzzes with guesses. Colonel Maynard's household sits at the center of post society. His young wife is new to army life.

Gossip, duty, and courtship fill the days that follow. Officers and ladies trade theories about the shooting. Alice Renwick appears in the later action, singing in the woods. A young officer's feeling for her breaks through his reserve. King knew the frontier army from his own service. The novel mixes mystery with a garrison romance.
george-borrow-the-man-and-his-books:
Edward Thomas published this study of George Borrow in 1912, drawing on Dr. Knapp's life of Borrow, on letters to the Bible Society, and on the work of other Borrow scholars. Borrow was a wanderer, linguist, and teller of wild tales, best known for Lavengro and The Bible in Spain. Thomas aims to show the man behind the books.

The study follows Borrow from his Norwich youth through his years on the road with Gypsies, his work selling Bibles in Spain, and his late, cranky fame. Portraits and pictures fill the book. Thomas writes with sympathy but keeps a critic's eye on Borrow's temper and tall stories. It is a good first map of a strange writer whose life reads like one of his own romances.
govdocs-archive_org--andras-laszlo-berse:
Andras Laszlo, a Hungarian traditionalist thinker, set down his Metaphysical Aphorisms in short, dense sayings. The collection appears in Hungarian, with sections in German. Laszlo wrote against the modern world from the standpoint of metaphysical tradition.

The aphorisms treat being, God, the universal subject, and what he calls the magical nature of existence, each in a few compressed lines. Aphorism suits his method: truth stated, not argued, for the reader to unfold. The set preserves hidden thought in bits, from a figure little known in English, and it serves readers who follow the traditionalist school in its Hungarian branch.
govdocs-archive_org-by-rene-guenon-berse:
René Guénon, the French writer who founded the Traditionalist school of thought, is represented here by The Veil of Isis, a collection of his essays. Guénon wrote on metaphysics and on the hidden doctrines he believed stood behind the world's religions.

The essays treat initiatic societies and esoteric teaching, and they include pieces on figures such as F.-Ch. Barlet and Sédir and on the Compagnonnage, the French craft brotherhoods. Throughout, Guénon judges modern occult groups against what he took to be genuine tradition, and he is rarely gentle. The collection is a key doorway into his thought.
govdocs-archive_org-d-herman-wirth-berse:
Herman Wirth was a Dutch-German scholar of prehistory who argued that the roots of mankind's religions and symbols lay in an ancient northern civilization. The Beginning of Mankind sets out that thesis, the central claim of his life's work.

Wirth reads rock carvings, calendars, and symbols as records of a primal faith carried outward from the far north by early peoples. His ideas won him a leading place in Nazi-era research; he co-founded the Ahnenerbe, the SS research institute. The work is hotly debated and held without endorsement, as a document of that era's scholarship on Aryan origins.
govdocs-archive_org-e-bruno-cariou-berse:
Bruno Cariou's essay Masquerade opens with Voltaire and with Giorgio Agamben, the Italian philosopher who wrote sharply on medicine and the power of the state. From that ground the essay builds into a polemic on the present day.

Cariou argues that the response to the Covid virus was a viral masquerade: a show of emergency that let governments rule by decree and turned medicine into an arm of the state. He writes in the French polemical tradition, literary and biting at once. The piece is a record of dissenting thought from the pandemic years.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JacksonDouglasD:
Dallas policeman Douglas Jackson rode escort in the presidential motorcade on November 22, 1963. His first-person account, titled I Saw the President Assassinated, begins with the 6:45 a.m. detail. It follows his duty through the morning and into the shooting itself.

Motorcycle and patrol escorts saw the motorcade from inside it. Jackson's account gives that view in a participant's own words, from the routine of the early detail to the moment the day broke apart. Firsthand officer narratives like his became basic sources for everyone who later rebuilt those minutes, block by block and turn by turn.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KennedyBooks_Ke: Kennedy Books: the fragmentary garbled text apparently from a discussion of Kennedy-killing books. Damaged, but kept, complete. A single fragment, filed. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-r-eddison-1922-berse:
E. R. Eddison published The Worm Ouroboros in 1922, before modern fantasy had a name. The story follows lords of Demonland as they wage war against Witchland on a world called Mercury.

Eddison wrote in a high, archaic prose modeled on old sagas and romances. Battles, feasts, quests, and proud speeches fill the book, and its heroes fight for honor more than for good. Along with a few rivals, the novel founded modern heroic fantasy, and writers such as Tolkien knew it well. The full text here keeps that founding work in print.
govdocs-archive_org-woman-problems-sieg-: Sieg Grun titled his work Woman Problems, and it appears here in a Berserker Books edition. The library holds it as an archive item and takes no stance on its contents. Beyond the author name and title, the record offers little that can be stated with confidence. The volume is preserved as part of the archive's holdings of polemical writing, where it documents its author and moment more than it argues a case a reader can test.
hearts-and-masks:
Harold MacGrath wrote this light adventure novel, first put out in 1905. The narrator falls in with a masked-ball set and a young woman in a Columbine costume. A house party, a hunt for a prize, and a string of small thefts pull him in deeper than he planned.

Much of the fun comes from hidden faces and false names. Guests hide who they are, clues turn up in odd places, and talk stays quick and playful. The plot moves through ballrooms, dark halls, and night searches. Readers who like early popular fiction with romance and mild peril will find a brisk, cheerful tale here.
invisible-links:
Selma Lagerlof wrote the tales in Invisible Links, rendered from the Swedish by Pauline Bancroft Flach. Lagerlof was already known for The Story of Gosta Berling. Contents list The Spirit of Fasting and Petter Nord, The King's Grave, and The Outlaws. A fallen king and a Christmas guest appear later.

The first tale recalls a small town known in every hole and corner. Its folk swell with pride at the smallest adventure, Lagerlof writes. A conqueror in another tale boasts that all within sight torture one another for gold. Legends and home tales mix in her early, lyrical manner.
juliana-horatia-ewing-and-her-books:
Juliana Horatia Ewing and Her Books is Horatia K. F. Eden's memoir of her sister, the children's writer. Eden, born Gatty, adds a selection of Ewing's letters to the life. Both parts run in time order, so readers can turn between memoir and letters. The book came out under the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge.

Eden warns that the letters were never meant for publication. They run full of family expressions and small allusions that strangers may find trivial. Yet they show Ewing's zeal, as in her method for teaching a liturgical class thirty-two years earlier. A letter on class singing shows her keen sense of musical rhythm. She wrote words for music though she could play no instrument.
just-folks:
Just Folks is a book of verse by Edgar A. Guest, dedicated to the Little Mother and the memory of the Big Father. The title poem opens the collection: 'We're queer folks here.' Guest's speakers talk of weather, good times, roses, and bees. They refuse, on principle, to scatter tales that harm their neighbors.

The home in these poems keeps one rule: be pleasant. Friends are treated as always present, so no one speaks ill of them. Guest wrote in plain, rhyming language about home, work, children, and kindness. Newspapers across America carried his verses to millions of ordinary readers. This collection shows why they called him the people's poet.
mavericks:
William MacLeod Raine wrote Mavericks, a western novel printed in 1911 and 1912. Grosset and Dunlap sold the book in New York. The front picture shows a rider twisted in his saddle, watching his back trail.

Phyllis leads the cast, and a nester comes in chapter two. A man is caught red handed in chapter three. The next head quotes a charge: I am a rustler and a thief, am I? Aid for a friend and a shot from ambush raise the stakes fast. A good friend and an aider stand in the later heads. Raine builds his range tale round theft charges and split loyalties.
narrative-and-legendary-poems-complete-v:
John Greenleaf Whittier's first collected volume holds his narrative and legendary poems. This Standard Library Edition was revised with the poet's own help. Whittier added head-notes giving each poem's subject and occasion. Dates of first printing fix when each piece was written.

The publishers added early poems Whittier had once discarded. Those sit in an appendix to the final poetry volume. Students of his career gain rich material here, they boast. The poems retell New England legends, history, and folk tales in verse. Whittier's plain, warm ballad style made such tales live for readers far beyond his Quaker home.
nonsense-books:
Edward Lear's Nonsense Books, issued in 1894 with all his original illustrations, gather his comic works in one place. A publishers' notice dates the first Book of Nonsense to 1846. Nonsense Songs and Stories followed in 1871, and More Nonsense Pictures in 1872. Laughable Lyrics closed the set in 1877.

John Ruskin is quoted at length in praise of the first book. He calls it the most beneficent and innocent book yet produced. Its carols, he says, are inimitable, refreshing, and perfect in rhythm. Ruskin knew no author to whom he was half so grateful for his idle self. He put Lear first among his hundred authors.
on-the-choice-of-books:
Thomas Carlyle's writings on books are gathered in this edition. A life of the author opens the volume. His Edinburgh address of April 2, 1866 follows. Carlyle spoke to students on choosing and using books. A farewell letter and his bequest close the book.

The introduction says genius ripens slowly toward fame. Carlyle lived at Great Cheyne Row from 1834 onward. He died in that house, the picture note adds. His address urges students to read great books deeply. Books, for Carlyle, were a true university for all. The volume preserves his voice as teacher and prophet.
one-day-a-sequel-to-three-weeks:
Elinor Glyn's circle produced this sequel to Three Weeks. The Macaulay Company first published it in 1909. This edition appeared in New York in 1912. It was issued anonymously at its first publication. Prince Paul receives a stiff royal letter in chapter one.

The letter arranges his marriage to Princess Elodie of Austria. His coronation will follow his twenty-first birthday in May. His uncle, Grand Duke Peter, signed the letter as regent. The prince scowls at the crown and the cold commands. He asks who this Princess Elodie is, anyway. Romance and court duty are set to collide.
one-hundred-best-books-with-commentary-a:
John Cowper Powys published this reading guide in 1916. It opens with an essay called Books and Reading. Powys imagines a young person who has read nothing. Such a question excites a man of letters, he says. Then the goblin of responsibility lifts its head.

Deep thought brings him back to his first impulse, he finds. The key is teaching aesthetic austerity in reading, he argues. A new reader needs the right mood and temper first. Reading is a voyage toward the Fortunate Islands, he suggests. His list names one hundred best books with commentary. The book guides beginners toward great literature with zeal.
podcast-dannyjones-I7CPUNSlXKs:
The Museum of Tarot channel's researchers join Danny Jones to break down new radar scans of the Giza plateau, which enthusiasts say reveal vast structures beneath the pyramids. Along the way, the conversation veers into military lasers that appear to communicate, a topic the guests connect to their wider reading of hidden technology.

The scans, known as SAR readings, have fueled a wave of claims about underground complexes at Giza. The guests explain their interpretation of the data image by image. Geologists and Egyptologists dispute those interpretations strongly, and no excavation has confirmed them. The episode preserves the claimants' walkthrough in full, which is what its audience came for. Listeners can follow the images' story and keep their own counsel on how much stone a radar echo can bear.
podcast-dannyjones-KScKEyhgmks:
Giampiero Ambrosi joins Danny Jones to tell a story that joins art history to espionage. It starts with a Leonardo da Vinci painting that sold for 450 million dollars. It extends to what Ambrosi calls the CIA psyops woven into modern art itself. The sale of Salvator Mundi, the most expensive artwork ever auctioned, anchors his suspicions.

Ambrosi works outward from the painting's shadowy path to a broader claim. He argues that intelligence agencies used abstract art as a Cold War weapon. That charge has some documented history behind its mildest form. His strongest claims go well past that record and are his own. Jones follows the money and the mystery with evident pleasure. Listeners get an art-world conspiracy narrated by a man who has chased it for years, preserved for its intrigue and its method alike.
podcast-joerogan-QBEZhjnZTks:
Jordan Peterson returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2308, another long entry in their years of talks. Peterson, the Canadian psychologist and author, draws some of the show's biggest audiences. His visits tend to range across everything he is thinking about at once.

The conversation moves through his current themes: meaning, faith, politics, and the state of young men, in his dense and urgent style. Rogan gives him long runs and jumps in with the questions his listeners would ask. The episode is a wide-ranging state-of-Peterson address, useful for tracking how his public argument has shifted over time.
podcast-joerogan-p1GONgRrdKs:
Government pressure on social media companies is the topic of this Joe Rogan Experience segment. It focuses on claims that intelligence and law enforcement agencies worked inside major platforms. The talk draws on reporting about back-channel requests and flagged posts.

Rogan and his guest go through how agencies are said to have asked platforms to remove or limit certain content. They debate where public safety ends and hidden censorship begins. Examples from recent news fights over speech online anchor the claims. For listeners worried about who controls what they see, the segment lays out the case in plain terms.
poetical-works:
Charles Churchill's poetical works come with a memoir, critical dissertation, and explanatory notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan. Gilfillan opens the life with a verdict: Churchill had powers that might have made him a poet. Hero, man, and saint, yet became instead a satirist, an unfortunate politician, and a profligate who died early. Readers, he says, must approach the corpse as they approach Burns and Byron, with sorrow, wonder, admiration, and blame mixed together.

Churchill, born in Westminster in February 1731 and schooled at Westminster. Rose with the Rosciad to become the most feared verse satirist in London, flaying actors, politicians, and Scots with rhymes all England repeated. Gilfillan's Victorian edition judges the life sternly while preserving the work whole, a combination that tells readers as much about the editor's age as about the poet's.
prefaces-and-prologues-to-famous-books:
Charles W. Eliot included this volume in his Harvard Classics, the famous five-foot shelf of books. Published by Collier in New York in 1909 and 1910, gathering the prefaces and prologues to famous books with introductions, notes, and illustrations. The idea is Eliot's in miniature: before the masterpieces, read what their makers said at the door. William Caxton dominates the early contents, with prologues to the Recuyell of the Histories of Troy, the Golden Legend, Malory's King Arthur, Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, and his Aesop.

Calvin's dedication of the Institutes follows, then Copernicus dedicating the Revolutions of the Heavenly Bodies, John Knox, and Spenser's prefatory letter to Sir Walter Raleigh on the Faerie Queene. Few anthologies teach so much literary history per page: printing, Reformation, the new astronomy, and epic all introduce themselves in their authors' own threshold words.
queer-little-folks: Queer Little Folks, by Harriet Beecher Stowe, is shown here in the London edition of T. Nelson and Sons, 1897, by title page and contents. The nine tales are animal stories. The Hen that Hatched Ducks opens the list. The Nutcrackers of Nutcracker Lodge and The History of Tip-Top follow. Miss Katy-Did and Miss Cricket appears. So does Mother Magpie's Mischief. The Squirrels that Live in a House is there. Hum, the Son of Buz and Our Country Neighbours follow. The Diverting History of Little Whiskey closes the list.
quotations-from-john-l-motley-works: Quotations from John L. Motley is a Widger's Quotations volume drawn from the Project Gutenberg edition of Motley's History of the Netherlands. The pages shown hold David Widger's editor's note and the opening of his contents. Widger invites readers to test whether their favorite passages are listed and to suggest more. The contents march through the Rise of the Dutch Republic in dated parts, from the introduction and 1555 onward through the 1570s.
quotations-from-the-project-gutenberg-ed: Quotations from the Works of Mark Twain stands first in the Widger's Quotations series, by David Widger. The pages shown are the Project Gutenberg header of an early file. It warns that proofing methods were then undeveloped. It points readers to an improved edition of the title. That edition is ebook number 7556. The header prints the series title, the copyright cautions, and the usual welcome to readers, before any Twain extracts begin.
ragged-dick-or-street-life-in-new-york-w: Ragged Dick, or Street Life in New York with the Boot-Blacks, by Horatio Alger, Jr., is shown here by its contents, dedication, and the first line of its preface. Twenty-seven chapters follow Dick from his introduction through Johnny Nolan, Dick's New Suit, The Pocket-Book, a room on Mott Street, fights with Micky Maguire, a tutor and first lessons, to a conclusion. The book is inscribed to Joseph W. Allen, at whose suggestion, the preface begins, the story was undertaken as a serial.
real-folks:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney published this work of fiction in 1893, in twenty-two chapters with names such as Luclarion, Hazel's Inspiration, and Morning Glories. The story opens in a city house where blinds are shut and windows shaded against the day. Two little girls slip out of a pantry window with their books.

They settle on a shed roof under a tall fir tree, in a spot Luclarion had passed over for a place down on the bricks. Later chapter titles promise news reaching Homesworth, talk overheard in Aspen Street, and questions and answers among neighbors and kin. Whitney builds her tale from home scenes, small choices, and the pull between town ways and plain living.
remarks:
Bill Nye, whose full name was Edgar W. Nye, filled this book of humorous remarks with more than one hundred and fifty pictures by J. H. Smith. A verse by Bret Harte about Ah Sin stands at the front. Nye's own directions open the fun: the book, he says, is for all classes of people.

It is, he boasts, a universal storehouse of thought, though thoughts he judged better left unthought were cut. That pruning, he claims, shrank the book to the thickness of an outspoken clergyman's bank book. He calls it his fourth book, issued only when public clamor grew too loud to ignore.
songs-from-books:
Rudyard Kipling says in his preface to Songs from Books that he has drawn together near all the verses and chapter-heads scattered through his books. Where a song was first used in a few lines alone, he gives it here in full. Macmillan at London printed the book, first in October 1913, with fresh printings in October and November 1913 and in 1914.

The first poem, Cities and Thrones and Powers, sets the tone. Cities, thrones, and powers stand in time's eye about as long as flowers, which die each day. Yet as new buds come forth to glad new men, cities rise again out of the spent and slighted earth. The figure gives Kipling's tales a grave frame: empires pass, and the life of men, like the year's flowers, comes back in fresh shapes.
tacitus-germania-agricola-brooks:
Tacitus, Rome's greatest historian, wrote two short works early in his career, around 98 CE. H. B. Brooks translated the Germania and the Life of Agricola. Both books look outward to Rome's northern frontier.

The Germania describes the tribes beyond the Rhine, their customs, assemblies, and warfare. Tacitus uses German simplicity to criticize Roman luxury by contrast. The Agricola honors his father-in-law, who governed Britain and won battles there. It mixes biography, ethnography, and a defense of honorable service under tyranny. Terse and moralizing, the pair shows Tacitus learning his craft. Brooks renders the compressed Latin faithfully.
tenterhooks:
Ada Leverson published Tenterhooks in 1912 as book two of her Little Ottleys tales, with a warm note to Robert Ross. Chapter one, A Verbal Invitation, finds Edith Ottley unwell and her husband Bruce keen to match her state.

Bruce, away at Carlsbad for his own aches, gets a letter from Edith full of care for his cure. She floats the name Matilda for their new girl, after a rich and holy aunt whose favor may aid the child. Edith then paints the two-day-old babe as a tall, golden-haired beauty with a gift for music. Readers get Leverson's dry, fond satire of smart London married life, where love, vanity, and money tangle in each small talk.
the-aeroplane-speaks:
H. Barber, a captain in the Royal Flying Corps, wrote The Aeroplane Speaks and gave it to the junior flying officer. In a front note on his motive, Barber says he wants to help the plain man grasp the aeroplane and the joys and troubles of its pilot.

He also aims to give hands-on help to the pilot and to the rigger, the pilot's key aide. Eight years spent designing, building, and flying aeroplanes back his claim to know the craft. He jokes that his hand knows the joy-stick far better than the pen. The prologue first ran in the Field in May 1916. Readers get plain talk on lift, rigging, and flight from the war's early air age.
the-babes-in-the-wood-one-of-r-caldecott:
R. Caldecott's picture book, printed in Great Britain by Frederick Warne, retells an old ballad in verse and pictures. Parents are asked at the start to ponder a sad story brought to light. A gentleman of good standing in Norfolk falls sick, and his wife lies sick beside him.

Both parents die and leave two small children, a boy not yet three and a younger girl. The father leaves his son three hundred pounds a year when he comes of age. Illustrations break up the verses, including one showing the parents near death, making the old tale plain for young readers.
the-black-baronet-or-the-chronicles-of-b:
William Carleton set Irish chronicles around a mail coach arriving by night. Chapter two describes a town and its inhabitants. Chapter three gives Paudeen Gair's recipe for making a bad dinner good and shows a stranger finding Fenton as mysterious as himself.

An anonymous letter follows, and Lucy Gourlay admits a previous attachment. Her father Sir Thomas fails to unmask the stranger and tries by falsehood to force Lucy to name her lover. A fortune-teller gives an equivocal prediction. Later headings name a visit to Father MacMahon and Crackenfudge outwitted by Fenton, while the baronet, enraged at his daughter's firmness, strikes her.
the-brother-clerks:
Xariffa wrote The Brother Clerks; A Tale of New-Orleans, put out in New York by Derby and Jackson in 1857. Verse lines on stranger lips and stranger eyes head the first chapter. A September sun casts its parting rays over the dull waters of the Mississippi. A steamer ploughs through the thick waves and rounds to at the thronged, busy wharf of New Orleans.

On her deck, apart from all the other passengers, stand two youths. They gaze with anxious eyes on the vast city spread before them. The taller and elder bears on his brow the flush of his twentieth summer. His hair is of that purplish black seen rarely save in a raven's wing or the portraits of old masters. A broad forehead, clear black eye, and red lips over snowy teeth make, the tale says, a picture of fresh and manly beauty.
the-ethics-of-george-eliot-s-works:
John Crombie Brown's The Ethics of George Eliot's Works, in a fourth edition from Blackwood dated 1884, began as a paper too long for any magazine. In Brown's last illness, talk turned to Eliot, the lost paper came up, and a critic friend's praise set it on the road to print. Brown meant to add Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda to round the work.

Death cut that plan short, and the book stands as friends left it. Brown reads Eliot's tales for their moral teaching: duty, sympathy, and slow growth. The study shows how the Victorians took their greatest novelist as a sage.
the-farmer-s-boy-one-of-r-caldecott-s-pi:
R. Caldecott drew this picture book of The Farmer's Boy, one of his famed toy books, printed in Great Britain by Frederick Warne. Song verses and big pictures share each page.

A boy sings of his days as a farmer's lad. First he keeps his master's horses, with a gee-wo here and a gee there. Then come the lambs, with baa-baa calls mixed into the same tune. Each new beast adds its cry to the song, and the boy calls to a lass to come to the banks of the Aire. Small children learn the farm by sound, rhyme, and Caldecott's lively art.
the-house-that-jack-built-one-of-r-calde:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book version of the cumulative nursery rhyme appeared from Frederick Warne and Company in 1878 as one of R. Caldecott's Picture Books. The pages build the famous chain one link at a time, each verse repeating everything before it. First comes the house that Jack built, then the malt that lay in the house, then the rat that ate the malt.

Illustration markers crowd the text, since the pictures carry half the fun: each new animal or figure gets its own image before joining the pile. The cat that killed the rat arrives next, and the chain keeps growing in the same pattern. Generations of children learned the rhythm of accumulation from Caldecott's lively drawings, and his picture books helped change what illustrated books for the young could look like.
the-lure-of-san-francisco-a-romance-amid: Elizabeth Gray Potter and Mabel Thayer Gray wrote The Lure of San Francisco, subtitled A Romance Amid Old Landmarks. Paul Elder and Company published it in San Francisco under a 1915 copyright, with illustrations by Audley B. Wells. Only the title pages, the illustrations list, chapter summaries, and the first line of the opening chapter are present, so the romance does not appear. The illustrations list tours landmarks: the Mission, Prayer Book Cross, Lotta's Fountain, and Chinatown. The chapter promises the romance of Luis Argüello at the Mission church.
the-pedler-of-dust-sticks:
Mrs. Follen wrote The Pedler of Dust Sticks, with illustrations by Billings. The contents list the title tale plus verses and pieces such as The Mighty Deeds of ABC, What Day Is It?, The Child at Her Mother's Grave, and Evening Prayer. The title story begins with a visit to a friend from Hamburg, whose room holds a striking portrait framed by ornamental drawings in cane and whalebone.

The frame shows whip handles, canes, piano keys, and umbrellas, all fancifully arranged. The friend explains that the portrait is her father, kinder even than he looks. The little sticks around it tell how he began his noble life as a humble pedler of dust sticks. Follen builds a child's moral tale from a family keepsake.
the-riches-of-bunyan-selected-from-his-w: Jeremiah Chaplin selected passages from John Bunyan for the American Tract Society, publishing at New York in 1850 with an introductory notice by William R. Williams. Contents arrange the extracts under heads beginning with God, the Trinity, the Scriptures, and man, with subheads on glory, majesty, justice, holiness, sovereignty, providence, mercy, and faithfulness. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so the extracts themselves do not appear.
the-starbucks: Opie Read, author of The Jucklins and A Kentucky Colonel, published this novel with Laird and Lee of Chicago, entered for copyright in 1902 by William H. Lee. Only the title pages and the start of a contents list are present here. The opening chapters cover the people of the hills. Jim the preacher, getting acquainted, and the post office follow. The hill-country story itself does not appear.
the-three-clerks:
Anthony Trollope's Three Clerks is introduced here by W. Teignmouth Shore, who insists there is a proper mood and place for reading a novel. No spot suits Trollope better, he says, than under a tree in Kensington Gardens on a summer day. From the avenue he conjures the early Victorian atmosphere. Red-brick Kensington Palace stands there, where Princess Victoria was awakened to hear she was Queen. Ghosts of men in baggy trousers and women in crinolines church-parade by the water.

Shore promises the social historian will mine Trollope alongside early Punch for the period's manners. He even previews characters Clerk Charley wrote about, Lady Crinoline and Mr. Macassar Jones. The introduction is a small essay in nostalgia. Readers are seated in Trollope's own century before his three young government clerks make their entrance.
the-two-jungle-books: Rudyard Kipling's Two Jungle Books, in the Barnes and Noble edition of 2011, is represented here by its copyright page and the first book's contents. Those contents list Mowgli's Brothers, Kaa's Hunting, and 'Tiger! Tiger!'. The White Seal, 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,' and Toomai of the Elephants follow. Hunting songs and parade songs stand interleaved between the stories. The second Jungle Book's contents and every story lie beyond the pages present. Readers can see the architecture of Kipling's animal tales without meeting a single wolf.
the-university-of-hard-knocks:
Ralph Parlette built his book from a lecture he had delivered more than twenty-five hundred times. Audiences on lyceum courses, at chautauquas, teachers' institutes, clubs, and conventions kept asking for the talk in print. More than a million people, the publishers say, had already heard it across the United States.

Parlette warns that the writing keeps the spoken form, since an audience shapes a lecture that survives. His subject is the school of hard experience, named in the subtitle as the school that completes our education. Verses from Revelation and Shakespeare about the uses of adversity open the volume. A third edition is announced here, with two companion lectures in preparation.
three-weeks:
Elinor Glyn addressed American readers directly when her novel Three Weeks, first published in 1907, reached a new land. She complained that England's press misunderstood and misrepresented the book. For Glyn, the Lady was a deep study of a strange Slav nature beyond ordinary morality.

She compares her method to painting a tiger rather than a spaniel, keeping every instinct accurate. The Lady, sacrificed to a brutal husband, meets a young Englishman at Lucerne and loves him through Venice. Readers get Glyn's own defence of a scandalous romance about passion, influence, parting, death, and a child.
